speakeroldname: Mr. Herb Breau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE PUBLICITY EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
1. There are no subsidies granted under the Machinery Program (MACH) as this is a tariff remission program. The Machinery and Equipment Advisory Board receives approximately 18,000 applications for remission of duty annually and it would not be practical to list individually all the approved applications. However, each year the Public Accounts includes a listing of the numbers of the Orders-in-Council which approved remissions under the program, together with the total amount actually remitted under each remission order. *
2.	The Machinery Program came into effect on January 1, 1968, along with other changes in Canadian tariffs arising from the Kennedy Round. Under the program the duty otherwise payable on machines, accessories, attachments, control equipment, tools and components imported under Tariff Item 42700-1, may be remitted if such goods are not available from production in Canada. In the budget of June 18, 1971, the provisions of the Machinery Program were extended to importations under Tariff Item 41100-1 covering machinery for use in sawmills and logging. The objective of the program is to increase efficiency throughout Canadian industry by enabling machinery users to acquire advanced equipment at the lowest possible cost, while at the same time affording Canadian machinery producers tariff protection on what they manufacture. In addition, Canadian machinery producers are protected by a single statutory rate of duty which applies immediately when they are in a position to supply.
3.	Each year, a report of the results of the Machinery Program is published and distributed to manufacturers and users of machinery. The report covers imports of machinery not available from Canadian production, on which duty has been remitted, and which could represent new manufacturing opportunities. It provides a breakdown of the types of machinery being imported, their value and country of origin. The latest report covers imports of machinery during the year 1971.

speechtext: 1 and 2. The Department of Justice has no information regarding the language in which the 252 bills that were introduced by the government in the twenty-eighth Parliament were initially conceived. However, the practice has been for the original draft of a bill to be prepared in the first instance in English, after which a French version of the draft would be prepared for consideration by the legal officers in the French-speaking unit of the Legislation Section. Both drafts would then be considered from the point of view of their implications in relation to the civil law, and from the point of view of whether each version corresponded with the other version accurately. In numerous cases following the consideration of a draft by members of the French-speaking unit of the Legislation Section and following consultation with the English-speaking members, changes were made in the draft, either in the French or the English version, or in both versions. After these changes were made, a final draft bill in fully bilingual form was prepared for review by the Cabinet.

Whenever there is a revision in the methodology of computing price indexes, it has been, and it remains, the policy of Statistics Canada to (a) document, in published form, all details explaining such a revision in methodology; (b) and to publish comparisons of the revised and the unrevised series for a period of overlap, in order to show what the changes in a series would have been using either the unrevised or the revised methodology. subtopic: CANADA WILDLIFE BILL

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, May 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Davis that Bill C-131, respecting wildlife in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.

subtopic: CANADA WILDLIFE BILL
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR RESEARCH AND CONSERVATION AGREEMENTS, CONTRIBUTIONS TO COSTS AND PURCHASE, ACQUISITION OR LEASE OF LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-131 which recognizes the responsibility of the Government of Canada to protect our heritage in this nation in terms of wild animals and other resources that were here prior to our coming, some of which have almost disappeared. This bill recognizes, also, that it is important that, if we are to justify our occupation of this half of the North American continent we must look after those things that are naturally here, so that they will be available for our children, our grandchildren and those who come after

us who will develop and make Canada the great land that it has the capacity to become.
I commend the minister for the suggestion in this bill that the Canadian Wildlife Service will extend its work in research and pathology in connection with toxic substances and other matters affecting wild animals and wildlife generally. I hope the minister will deal with the serious question of trapping. I have received many letters from young children in my riding decrying the use of the leg-hold trap in the taking of wild animals by trappers and others, decrying the injuries caused to animals whose legs are torn off or they are trapped in these devices and suffer for days before their frozen bodies are picked up and taken to be skinned. We have now developed the Conibear trap, but even with it I understand there are problems in that it is heavy to move around and sometimes the effect of this trap, which is supposed to kill wild animals instantaneously, results in the whole of their face being mutilated. We need an investigation or inquiry into new forms of trapping that will not be as injurious to animals as the existing devices.
The work done by the minister in connection with migratory birds has been excellent. I hope that in developing the thesis behind this bill he will extend this conservation work to other forms of migratory animals, indeed to animals of the high seas in the northern part of Canada where sometimes it is difficult to know whether we own land or sea.
I commend the minister for bringing this whole matter to the attention of the House of Commons, but having inspected the bill I find that it is one the most loosey-goosey pieces of legislation to come before the House for some time. It gives the minister powers. It provides that he "may" do all sorts of things. He may undertake, promote and recommend measures; he may initiate conferences; he may undertake programs of research; he may establish advisory committees; he may co-ordinate and implement; he may take charge of this or carry out measures with respect to that. There is only one place in the bill where it says the minister "shall" do anything. That is in clause 11, which provides that the minister shall spend wisely money given to him, in accordance with the provisions laid down when it is given to him.
What we are really doing in this legislation is giving the minister authority to conduct almost any kind of program that he wishes. The minister can go charging off in one direction one day; the next day he can determine that that is not his priority and go charging off in another direction. At no time is he under any obligation to come back to the House of Commons and say what the priorities should be and where the limited amount of social capital available should be used in promoting and doing something for the preservation of wildlife.
I think it is high time we established some mandatory priorities. The minister should bring legislation before the House in which he says, "Members of Parliament, I want to do certain things and these are my priorities. These are the wildlife species I want to preserve. This, Members of Parliament, is the problem and this is specifically what I am asking you to authorize me to do." But legislation in this loosey-goosey fashion is not fair to the House and is not fair to the people of Canada.

There are provisions in the bill under which agreements can be made with the provinces for joint undertakings and agreements can be made with private organizations, with the permission of the provinces. I think it is proper that the minister should have permission to make certain agreements but we must ask, what kind of agreements? Agreements to do what; to preserve what? To say "just to preserve wild animals," in the total picture, is not definitive enough. It does not specifically set out to the House what the minister is really going to do. What we have is motherhood legislation. Wild animals are popular, it is nice to have a bill on wildlife, so we have a nice bill on wildlife that does not say a darn thing.
There is one problem that really disturbs me about this bill. It comes with clause 13, which provides that the governor in council may make regulations prohibiting certain things, specifying measures, and so on. The clause 14 reads:
Every person who violates any provision of this act or the regulations-
Mr. Speaker, there are no compulsory or mandatory provisions in the bill, so clause 14 must mean regulations. -is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
What we have is criminal law introduced with criminal sanctions upon summary conviction, without even the regulations, rules or even the aims and objects of the regulations and rules brought before the House of Commons. The minister may make a regulation, he may even make a regulation to cover something that happened in the past, and the person who broke that regulation would be guilty of an offence and subject to punishment upon summary conviction. This kind of thing should not appear in legislation; it is the type of activity that should be stricken from this bill. If the minister has rules and regulations and if they are to carry with them penal results, they should be set out in detail so that the people of Canada know what laws they are likely to break.
I want to make some suggestions with respect to this bill, Mr. Speaker. I think it should set out in detail the extent of federal government involvement in the preservation of wildlife. It should set out in detail to what extent it is a matter of federal authority and to what extent the federal government is looking to the provinces, the counties and the territories of Canada to do their part under the legislation.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, federal responsibility clearly encompasses those animals and birds subject to large migration, and in particular migration across provincial boundaries. That may well apply to the caribou herd and presumably it applies to whales in our inland seas. It may well apply to other animals and birds with which I am not too familiar, although I am sure the minister has in his department people who are familiar with them.
The whole question of wildlife in the territories should be brought under this legislation. In answer to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) last night, I presume the minister was really saying that wildlife in the territories is a matter for the territorial council. Mr. Speaker, the territories are not yet provinces. I suggest that the assets and resources of the territories belong to all
Wildlife Protection
of Canada; thus they are the direct responsibility of the minister and should be specifically set out as being within the federal competence. The minister should also make it quite clear that it is a federal responsibility to co-ordinate research carried out by provincial and other authorities in connection with wildlife. To some extent that is contained in this bill, but it is not clear and specific.
The whole question of wildlife within federal parks is a loose one. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) is responsible for federal parks and apparently has staff looking after wildlife in those parks. But we should have one minister to look after wildlife problems in Canada. Surely, if we are going to have a wildlife act it should set out that the Minister of the Environment is responsible for wildlife in all federal parks and all federal public lands.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I think the legislation should set out what the endangered species are, and it should set out clearly what the minister should do and is directed to do with respect to the preservation of those endangered species. When legislation provides for a grants system to provinces and private organizations, surely this House should have an opportunity to know what kind of grants the minister has in mind. Perhaps the legislation should be specific and set out the type of projects that the federal treasury will sponsor or in which it will share the costs of the provinces and private organizations. In my opinion and in the opinion of some others it is not good enough to give the minister the right to make grants or agreements, because it leaves the whole matter open to the question of who knows whom; who has a project; is money available, if so, make an application and if it is politically sound, money will be made available. This is just not good enough, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in the NDP-and my remarks do not pertain exclusively to my group-have for a long time been concerned about wildlife and wildlife management. We are concerned about preserving the natural habitat of wildlife in this land and the respect that should be paid to nature itself. We appreciate the bill and realize that it tends to deal with an area that is largely under provincial legislation not only with respect to wildlife but to many matters which affect wildlife. For instance, provincial governments have jurisdiction over general questions involving land and land use or the misuse of land. That area of concern has an effect upon wildlife. The question of waters under provincial jurisdiction also may involve matters which have serious effects upon wildlife. Activities involving forestry, logging, mining, recreation in provincial parks and camping grounds, hunting, fishing and logging which come under the jurisdiction of the provinces impinge in one way or another upon species of wildlife.
In his opening statement the minister indicated that this bill has been the subject of discussion with provincial governments and that each of the ten provinces has endorsed it. I did not grasp clearly, from what the minister said last night in response to a question asked by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), the relationships involving the federal government, this bill and the territorial governments of the Yukon and Northwest Territories. The minister intimated that the approach taken with respect to those territories was the same as that taken with respect to the provinces, but his statement was

not clear and I think requires clarification. To my mind, at least, there ought to be a clearer understanding of how this bill involves the territories, particularly in light of oil and natural gas discoveries in the northern areas and the dangers that those discoveries can bring not only to wildlife but to the terrain itself.
I am of the opinion that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development should not be given jurisdiction, under this bill, with respect to national parks; I do not think there ought to be duplication of responsibility in these areas at the federal level. I think we should make that clear now. This legislation ought to apply to wildlife in the national parks, otherwise two approaches to protection may be taken and the matter may involve different jurisdictions.
The pressures upon wildlife in this land are very large, very impressive, very dangerous and largely unknown. The bulk of our population are city folk. They live in an urban setting. I do not say this in an unkind way. However, people who live in rural areas come in contact daily with nature and know more of nature than do people who live in cities. As I said, the bulk of our population lives in cities and works in cities and only rarely, at vacation time or the odd weekend, are city people able to go to the country. So, often they do not really understand what wildlife is and do not have adequate knowledge of it. In the sense that we do not understand the effects of all aspects of human activity, the pressures on wildlife are largely unknown.
Sometimes we build dams, as happened in my province, as the minister knows, and we create artificial lakes, thereby flooding thousands of acres. Sometimes we flood moose pasture and elk pasture and destroy food sources for antlered animals. This tends to kill them off or drive them away to other areas. This, in turn, creates additional pressures on foods available in other areas. Also, the operations of logging companies drive fur-bearing animals from the area. The consequences of indiscriminate logging, coupled with dry summers and forest fires, create additional dangers to animals and birds in the forests.
Although hunting from helicopters is not permitted or authorized under provincial law, as I understand it, one hears of hunters using helicopters to hunt. They may come either from within or without Canada. These people are able to charter helicopters, and they fly around the mountain tops and ridges and pick off mountain sheep and goats as if catching the proverbial fish in the proverbial barrel. This sort of indiscriminate hunting indulged in for the acquisition of heads and horns, and not for meat, indulged in because the hunter simply wishes to kill something, continues and endangers the wildlife of this land.
We are familiar from reading, if by no other way, of the effects of pesticides, herbicides, chemicals and effluents which are discharged by industrial plants. We know that fertilizers which used to contain phosphates and detergents have been flushed down into the ocean where they have contaminated fish and birds who feed upon those fish. Those chemicals are destructive and injurious. Therefore, because we must concern ourselves about these matters we endorse the principles contained within the bill.
We know that because in this country there are different provincial jurisdictions, one set of rules and concepts
May 9, 1973_________________COMMONS DEBATES________________________3579
will apply in one province and may not apply in another. These concepts at the provincial level may alter from time to time. The provinces may adopt more rigid views at any given moment in preserving wildlife, or their thinking may become not so rigid. There is a good thought within the bill to the effect that we may be able to develop-and I hope we will-uniformity of concept with respect to preserving wildlife throughout all the provinces and territories.
I am a bit unhappy that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is to be free to go its own way, because that way may or may not coincide with the way the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) wants to go. Apart from that, I am a bit unhappy about the provisions of clause 9, which provides that the minister may, in co-operation with one or more provincial governments, do certain things. I assume from what the minister said last night that he conceives that to also mean in co-operation with the territories, but the bill does not say that and I think it excludes it. I would like to know just what that clause means. In any event, it provides that the minister may, in co-operation with the provinces, take whatever measures he deems necessary for the protection of any species of non-domestic animal in danger of extinction.
The phrase "in danger of extinction" is not clear. It makes one think that only when a species of wildlife reaches the stage of being in danger of extinction will a move be made to correct the situation. In many ways, when that state of affairs is conceived and understood, it is too late; the damage has been done. We all know of species which make an almost superhuman effort just to keep alive the process of propagation.
I would like to see the clause altered so that it does not carry the implication that we only move at the last possible moment. That is what the phrase "in danger of extinction" means to me. It does not give any clear indication of the basis for deciding whether a species of wildlife is in danger of extinction. Also, the bill does not take into account what species of wildlife may be in danger of extinction in one area or another. I refer, for example, to islands. Some species are peculiar to certain islands. Any undue hunting, industry, use of pesticides, helicopters, or any of the other things I mentioned earlier, such as mining and logging operations, could not only place wildlife in the area in danger of extinction but could extinguish it completely.
There are areas of northern British Columbia where the grizzly bear is now extinct. Because of new roads and people, he is moving farther and farther away. Even though we have different ideas about the grizzly bear, it is a rather shy animal, as are most animals in the forest. They want to keep out of our way as much as we want to keep out of theirs. When an animal hears a person in the bush, it gets out of his way; it is not interested in meeting him. Because of road building, logging and aircraft, more people are moving into these remote areas.
Grizzly bears are feared and hunted. This is the concept we have of someone who is hunting a grizzly bear. It is ridiculous, because usually the hunter is in a blind in a
Wildlife Protection
tree some distance from the grizzly bear. He has a high-powered rifle with a powerful telescope. The poor grizzly bear, hundreds of yards away, does not have a clue what is going on until he has been shot. The "fearless" hunter then climbs down from his safe position and collects his trophy of a grizzly bear head or skin. This lack of respect for wildlife is indicative of what is happening to species such as the grizzly bear.
This is also true of black bears. In many respects they are very gentle souls. They wander all over the streets of Jasper and Banff. They are a bit of a nuisance at times because they scrounge from garbage pails. However, they have some protection. When they wander along the road they are likely to be shot by someone travelling in a car. The purpose is merely to cater to that individual's desire to kill something.
The words contained in clause 9, which imply that action will be taken only when animals are in danger of extinction, should be changed. Action should be taken before that time in order to preserve our wildlife. Also, there should be research with regard to preserving wildlife species so they may grow and develop. There is a need for herds to enlarge. Such research should take into account not only biological questions which impinge upon propagation of the species, but harvesting for food and hunting for trophy purposes. I am not the least bit interested in supporting the idea of trophy hunting. In fact, I would like to see the federal and provincial governments promote the idea of people hunting with a camera instead of a gun. This would attract a different group of people from those with the killer instinct. I would like to see people preserve on film what they see, rather than having a moose head on the wall, collecting dust, to which a hunter can point with pride. In most cases these poor, defenceless animals are shot from a distance of great safety.
In addition to the biological question, research should involve the economic question. With regard to hunting, there are a number of guides who earn their living guiding people into hunting areas. They earn their living by showing others what wildlife is all about. This research should involve recreational forest areas in a way similar to what I was saying about cameras a moment ago. I do not think the concept of research being carried out entirely within the minister's department or in conjunction with the provinces will be satisfactory. It would be much more fruitful if grants were made to people outside the government service to do research in this field. I cannot think of a group of people who know more about wildlife and are more intimately involved than our native Indian people. They know what wildlife is all about.
In this area, I believe extremely useful research work could be done if we were to draw on the experience of our native Indians. Grants for research work might also be given to guides and trappers who live a large part of their lives in the bush in the same habitat as the animals we now seek to protect, as well as to wildlife foundations, rod and gun clubs and other groups which by their activities have shown concern for the wildlife of this land.

May 9, 1973
Wildlife Protection
When the bill gets before the committee I hope it will not be rushed through. I hope an opportunity will be given for people whose lives are closely associated with nature and wildlife to make suggestions and representations for improving the measure, for making it function in a better way than is conceived from the point of view of the lawyers who drafted it or from the point of view of the minister who determined policy questions with regard to it. Legislation of this nature concerns itself with something beyond the normal comprehension of most of us in this House or, indeed, in our society today. We must draw on the knowledge, experience, feelings and understanding of those who of their own volition live a life which respects the wild creatures around them. If we do this, I am sure we can produce a measure which will be a credit to this land for a long time to come.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make some brief remarks on Bill C-131, an act respecting wildlife in Canada. I realize that it is just enabling legislation, but there are several points affecting the prairie provinces which I think should be stressed at this time. Many of the points contained in the bill came out of the Resources for Tomorrow Conference which was held over ten years ago. I am glad the government has brought forward this legislation because it is long overdue. All Canadians wish to do everything possible to preserve our wildlife. Nobody appreciates wildlife more than people who live in the rural areas of Canada, because they live so close to nature.
One concern I have about this legislation is that no mention is made of the dollars for wetlands program. This program was introduced by the Progressive Conservative government in the early sixties and was established to encourage farmers in the prairie provinces not to drain sloughs and potholes on their farms. I felt it was a very effective program. As we are all aware, in the early 1960s grain sales were good and farmers wishing to increase production were trying to put as much of their land under cultivation as possible. This meant that many potholes and sloughs were being drained. The situation became so serious that water tables in many areas were affected. Not only did this occur, but as these sloughs and potholes were vast breeding grounds for the duck population in North America there was a distinct possibility that if the trend continued it could result in the extinction of the ducks.
The government of the day was aware of this possibility and introduced the dollars for wetlands program. Under the program the government paid an annual incentive to farmers who agreed not to drain their land. The farmer was compensated for loss of income incurred through not putting land into forage or grain production. The program was very effective when it was introduced. However, in 1969 and 1970 the government at that time decided, for some unknown reason, that there should be a cutback in the program. The cutback was in fact so severe that very few farmers participated. Another problem was that no change had been made in the amount of incentive paid to farmers since the program was introduced. We are all aware of the increases in costs to our farmers, and at that time we urged the government to double the incentive paid because their rates were out of date. But the govern-
ment would not listen. The irony of the situation is that in the year that we saw the biggest cutback by the government in the dollars for wetlands program, we also saw the introduction of the program known as Lift.
Here was a situation in which one department of government was paying the farmer not to grow wheat and encouraging him to take the land out of production, while at the same time another department of government was discontinuing a very effective program which was achieving the same result in addition to protecting the environment. This paradox was brought to the attention of the government, but in their arrogant way members opposite would not listen. I hope the dollars for wetlands program is completely reinstated and that farmers will be paid enough compensation to encourage them to leave their sloughs undrained. The area of Manitoba which I represent is one of Canada's largest duck breeding grounds. If these breeding grounds are to continue to exist, farmers will have to receive proper compensation. I know they are prepared to co-operate.
Ducks feeding on farmers' crops in the field present a very real and costly problem on the Prairies. This has been mentioned in the House many times. As a result, because of their heavy losses a number of farmers view the duck population with concern. The government has, it is true, taken some steps to ease this situation. Farmers are sometimes criticized for the position they take in this regard, but I can imagine how loudly any retail merchant would holler if birds were allowed to eat produce off his shelves. If wildlife is to be protected, farmers will have to receive sufficient compensation for damage to their crops. This is a "must" if the bill is to be effective.
One other point I should like to make concerns damage by wildlife to crops which have been left in swath during the winter due to poor harvest weather. Riding Mountain National Park is in my constituency. It is more than 1,200 square miles in area. Many farms border the park or are in its vicinity. If these farmers are obliged to leave crops out in swath for long, the damage done by wildlife from the park is almost unbelievable. When they complain about their losses either to the province or to the federal government, each level of government claims it has no responsibility. I hope the bill before us will see that proper compensation is paid to farmers for damage done to crops by wildlife.

Mr. Speaker, in commenting on the bill before us I should like to address my remarks in particular to clause 9 to which my hon. friend from Skeena (Mr. Howard) was referring a while ago. If I might make a suggestion in all humility to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis), it would be that he consider looking at Bill C-165. My humility is, of course, increased as I note that this particular bill relates closely to a private member's bill submitted by myself for the consideration of the House. It is entitled "an act respecting the protection of endangered species." The material in that bill certainly relates closely to clause 9 of the bill we are presently studying. For the interest of the House I shall read the brief clause 9 of the bill before us. It is entitled "Endangered wildlife" and provides:
May 9, 1973

The minister may, in co-operation with one or more provincial governments having an interest therein, take such measures as he deems necessary for the protection of any species of non-domestic animal in danger of extinction.
I humbly submit, Mr. Speaker, that although the intention and the spirit of the clause are good, the clause is still a relatively weak one. As the expression often goes in this House, it is a provision without teeth. The only teeth that this provision would have are to be found in the mouths of the poor animals who are supposed to be protected. There are no specific provisions as to how action is to be taken. There is nothing in the clause about sanctions and there is, indeed, very little definition.
As a suggestion to the minister and to the committee I should like to put forward some distinctions and definitions which are contained in Bill C-165 which I think are more specific and useful. There is an attempt to define "endangered species" in this way:
-"endangered species" means any wild mammal, wild bird, amphibian or reptile which by regulation is declared by the minister to be threatened with extinction-
Further on there is a definition of that last phrase, "threatened with extinction":
-"threatened with extinction" means a species or subspecies which is either unlikely to continue to survive without special protective measures-
I think this underlines the point that the hon. member for Skeena was making so effectively.
-or occurs in such small numbers and/or in such a restricted or specialized habitat that it could easily disappear.
In other words, this kind of definition is, I think, more useful than the very general statement that is contained in the present bill and I think meets the kind of concern expressed by the hon. member for Skeena. However, it is not enough for us in Canada to think only of the wildlife of this country as isolated from the rest of the world. In this case as in so many others we must have an international approach to the concern we feel. It may be that practices followed in this country can have a nefarious effect on wildlife in other countries. In order to make my point 1 should like to read from an article that appeared in one of our daily newspapers this winter, from a United Press source. It is brief and reads as follows:
U.S. Attorney Robert Morse and Assistant Secretary of the Interior Nathaniel Reed said yesterday in Brooklyn federal court the largest ring of traffickers in illegal animal pelts ever uncovered had been smashed.
You might ask, quite rightly, Mr. Speaker, what are illegal animal pelts? How would we define them as being illegal in this country? I suggest it would be difficult since we do not have a law in this country that defines trafficking in certain animal pelts as illegal. The article continues:
A major company which admitted $5 million worth of purchases and sales of threatened species, including ocelot, otter, leopard, cheetah, jaguar and puma, faces a $500,000 fine.
That is a fairly stiff fine. But the next paragraph is the one that should really startle us:
Reed-
That is to say, the Assistant Secretary of the Interior, Nathaniel Reed.
-said these illegal pelts are shipped to storehouses in Canada and
Wildlife Protection
Switzerland because these countries do not now prevent the purchase and sale of these skins.
It is rather nice to have some international attention, but there are some times when we get attention that we could do without. This is certainly one of those times. Canada and Switzerland are about the only two countries left in the North Atlantic world, as it were, which do not prevent by law trafficking in skins and pelts of endangered species. I wish this bill did have some more teeth in it particularly with this point in mind.
Referring again to Bill C-165, which I submit is a better defined document, it contains a provision regarding international concern in the objects of the bill. The bill states:
It is hereby declared that it is necessary to assist on an international and domestic level in the preservation of species threatened with extinction and that there is illegal traffic on an international and national scale of skins of wild mammals, wild birds, amphibians and reptiles which threatens the survival of many rare species.
Again we have the balancing effect of supply and demand here: if we can cut off the supply, we will stop the demand-effectively. But as long as Canada remains a warehouse for this kind of trafficking it will always be possible for traffickers, whose trade is illegal in other countries such as the United States, to come to this country and set up operation. For this I do not think we should hold up our heads with too much pride.
I know I keep quoting from Bill C-165, Mr. Speaker, but there is this provision in the bill which is quite specific:
The minister
(a)	shall determine to the extent possible through consultation with foreign countries, interested persons and organizations what species and/or subspecies are threatened with extinction either on a worldwide basis or a habitat basis; and
(b)	may seek the advice and assistance of scientific organizations and specialists in the fields of zoology, ornithology, and herpetology, without restricting the range of advice and assistance to the said scientific fields.
Then in the operative part of the bill there is the provision that no person shall sell, purchase, store or import into Canada the skin of any endangered species. I think many members of this chamber would have more confidence in Bill C-131 if clause 9 contained provisions of the kind I have just cited from Bill C-165, where there is clear instruction as to how the minister is to proceed, what advice he is to seek, on what basis he may declare a species an endangered species, and there is a clear prohibition against the sale, trading, warehousing, exporting or dealing in the skins and pelts of endangered species. Then beyond the prohibition there is the calling for a sanction as follows:
Any person violating any provision of this act or any regulation is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction and liable for each offence to a fine of five thousand dollars and imprisonment to a term not exceeding five years or to both.
Put this kind of provision in the bill, Mr. Speaker, and obviously you will have teeth in it. Left as it is, I think clause 9 will do very little other than express finer sentiments. It does very little more than give vent to our feelings, offering no real likelihood of any effective action being taken.
It is very rarely in this House that we debate the interpretation part of a bill, but I should like to suggest

I suppose the obverse is true and that any domestic animal is one which is non-wildlife. You have a definition here which with its counterpart is, of course, completely tautological. It is comprehensive but it is not very deprecative. There are certain species that clearly fall either within one of these categories or within another of these categories.
