speechtext: The horse.

subtopic: CANADA WILDLIFE BILL
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR RESEARCH AND CONSERVATION AGREEMENTS, CONTRIBUTIONS TO COSTS AND PURCHASE, ACQUISITION OR LEASE OF LANDS
speechtext:
I hear my colleague from Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) exclaim from his bench, "The horse". In Canada we have domestic and wild horses, and there have been recent cases in the handling of horses both wild and domestic for export which should cause us to bow our heads in justifiable shame. Some time ago-I forget exactly when, but well over a year-the Department of Transport did inaugurate a fairly good code for shipboard transportation of horses. Members of this House may not be aware that horses are shipped live out of this country, ostensibly, in many cases, for the purpose of breeding and rearing in Europe, and in other cases for the purpose of slaughter. I understand that the code does stipulate in part that horses over II years of age may not be shipped out of the country for the purpose of slaughter.
Several societies concerned with the humane treatment of animals looked into these shipments and came away rather alarmed at the way these animals are treated on shipboard. It is obvious to anyone who looks into the situation that horses are shipped to Europe, there to be slaughtered and their flesh to be served on the tables of Europeans. If those people want to eat horse meat, I suppose that is their business. What we should be concerned with in this country is the situation when these animals are shipped out of Canada for this purpose.
I would take a much more simple approach to the matter, Mr. Speaker. I suggest that no horses should be shipped live out of this country for the purpose of slaughter overseas. Then we would know absolutely that these animals would be killed humanely here and that our handling of them would be sound and humane. No matter how well we supervise this-and I doubt that we do or can supervise it well-I do not suppose we will ever be able to assure ourselves that these animals are humanely treated once they have left the port of Montreal or Halifax and are on a ship somewhere in the middle of the Atlantic.
Horses can fall ill and die, and horses that are too old obviously cannot suffer the sea passage safely. Some horses may have foals that are too young to be treated in this fashion. Others simply have not been trained and are not sufficiently docile. Many horses have been reported to have been treated most inhumanely during shipment. Perhaps when we review this bill in committee we can consider the rather vague definition of "wildlife" and expand the bill to the consideration of this kind of situation.
Someone might tell me that my intervention is a little out of order, but I know there have been allegations made to the effect that wild horses from Alberta have been shipped to Europe under these conditions. If we want to

take that very sound view and make that distinction between wild and domestic animals, we should at least take steps to prevent this kind of inhumane treatment.
Let me end by saying there is something very biblical about this event. The expressed concern on the part of the government and hon. members of this House for the wellbeing of animals is something which dates back to the very beginning of biblical times. According to the first book of Genesis we were put on this earth to tend the garden, and we were expected to tend this garden with respect. In a very significant way, the manner in which we deal with the creatures with which we share this earth is a reflection upon ourselves. If I may interpret, as indeed has been done many times before, the first verse of Genesis, the first thing that Adam did was to name the animals. I suppose this is what the minister proposes we now do in a modern way. We are not going to name them, we are going to research them. Let us hope that our research goes beyond the mere expression of idle curiosity and becomes an expression of our concern for our fellow creatures on this earth.

subtopic: CANADA WILDLIFE BILL
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR RESEARCH AND CONSERVATION AGREEMENTS, CONTRIBUTIONS TO COSTS AND PURCHASE, ACQUISITION OR LEASE OF LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about this bill, and I congratulate the minister for bringing it in. In dealing with wildlife in Canada the bill covers many things. It provides for agreements with the governments of the provinces, so it covers provincial, municipal and township matters. It deals with organizations or persons associated with wildlife research. I think this is a very important matter as we are always faced with problems of research, particularly in the area of our wildlife kingdom. It deals with payments and contributions in respect of the cost of measures resulting therefrom, and provides for the purchase, acquisition or lease of lands. It also provides for the costs incurred in administration of the legislation to be paid out of moneys to be appropriated by parliament, and relates to other matters in connection with the administration of this legislation. I think this is a very good measure in that it deals with these aspects and covers a tremendous area of the country.
We all know what happens if we do not maintain the balance of wildlife in this country. We are also aware of the disappearance of many species of wildlife. We know there is a great deal of importance in maintaining this balance of life. I have in mind the fact that the wolf population in the northland kills the crippled, the lame, the halt and the blind of our caribou and deer populations. These animals would encounter untold suffering if it were not for wolves killing them humanely and mercifully. I think the ecology of the north would be very much upset, particularly in the Northwest Territories, if we did not have wolves to kill off the mice. Mice destroy all kinds of vegetation in that country. The same applies to foxes and rabbits, and one might include in that chain hawks who live on mice and other small animals, and other carnivorous species.
I should like to refer to an article which goes back to the 1950s when the Dutch elm disease threatened some of the trees which line the streets of many mid-western towns. In 1954, Michigan State University, which has a large number of elms on its East Lansing campus, began to spray with DDT to kill the beetles that spread the disease. The beetles began to die, but so did a large number of
May 9, 1973

robins. Soon zoologists discovered that earthworms ate the DDT-covered leaves that fell to the ground, the worms in turn were eaten by the robins, causing them to die of nerve poisoning. This example covers three species and stages in the ecological chain.
Michigan State's experience is a demonstration of the phenomenon known as biological magnification. While the DDT concentration in one area may be microscopically low, it can multiply through the food chain. Several birds along the Great Lakes, including the American eagle, were threatened with extinction because of the use of DDT, because DDT causes the liver to produce enzymes that attack the hormones governing the production of calcium. I should like to quote the following from the Globe and Mail of July 7, 1969:
When the eagle's system produces less calcium, the eggshells become thinner, causing more frequent breakage and fewer baby eagles.
The osprey, peregrine falcon and mallard duck have problems similar to those of the eagle. And the Minks Ranchers Association believes that DDT may be affecting mink reproduction.
I think this covers quite a field, and it goes to show how we can destroy wildlife by using controls such as pesticides. The article goes on to read:
Humans seem to eliminate DDT once it reaches a level of 10 or 12 parts per million. (Most North Americans apparently have that level in their bodies).
Experiments' in feeding prisoners massive DDT doses have uncovered no measurable dangers-
But in treating mice they did run into problems which showed that it might be harmful. The experiments also indicated that DDT might interfere with the productivity of wildlife.
I want to congratulate wildlife groups, people in fish and game clubs and rod and gun clubs for the part they have played. In my area there are such clubs, particularly fish and game clubs and conservation clubs, that have done very useful work. They have bought up land here and there and have stocked it with wild animals and birds. These animals and birds are multiplying under these normal conditions, just as if they were free. It is a beautiful sight to see these animals and birds, some of which are being released into the woods because of overpopulation. I cannot stress sufficiently the important part these organizations have played in building such sanctuaries. They have aroused public opinion, which is very important. Public opinion has been aroused on the very subject that the minister has been smart enough to put into legislation and bring before the House.
I want to refer for a minute or two to the remarks of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Stewart) who commented very ably on the wetlands and how they could be used. The same thing applies to Ontario, where we could protect our bush and similar areas that are unfit for agriculture but would make excellent havens for wildlife. The other day I was in the bush, a woodlot of about 200 acres. There were deer there, bears, raccoons and beavers; a stream goes through the lot. This was very interesting to me. Here was preservation of animals by people, without any compulsion at all. They did it because they like to protect the wildlife of the country.
Wildlife Protection
I would also like to refer to the comments of the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Harney) who dealt with the problem of wild and tame horses. This is certainly a problem that affects us all, and it probably distresses a good many people when horses are caught and shipped abroad. Many times they are injured on the way, and a few times they have had colts during shipment. One such case was reported to me, and when one case is reported there are usually many others. This matter could be taken care of by the federal branch dealing with the health of animals. As is the case when any type of thoroughbred or other animal is shipped out of the country, a health certificate should be required for the animal. Regulations could be brought in barring any animals from being shipped overseas that were not going there for breeding purposes. It is as simple as that. If there happened to be too many wild horses, they could be slaughtered, frozen and then shipped. Let us not do this by the back door in an underhand way. Let us be fair and honest in our approach to the problems connected with wild horses and wildlife.
In conclusion, I want to congratulate the minister. I know that he will have the support of all members of the House on his progressive legislation.

subtopic: CANADA WILDLIFE BILL
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR RESEARCH AND CONSERVATION AGREEMENTS, CONTRIBUTIONS TO COSTS AND PURCHASE, ACQUISITION OR LEASE OF LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on second reading of this bill. It is perhaps one of the few bills that will receive unanimous agreement from all sides of the House and from all the public. If there are any misgivings, they would only be that the bill does not go far enough and is not sufficiently extensive to satisfy many people.
In his speech the minister gave a good resume of what the bill hopes to accomplish. I think the public is becoming increasingly aware of what only a few generations ago only the conservationist was aware of, namely, that man as a species of animal himself must be increasingly aware of the fact that he is limited by many of the boundaries of nature within which other animal species are restricted, and that he is finding the same peripheries to his activities that nature applies to other animals.
The multiplication of a new species creates a new balance. This seems to have been true since the world began. Rather belatedly, the human species is realizing that the preservation of many animals is desirable and even necessary for our survival. Of course, we have our domesticated animals which have come from the wilds, but as well there are many other animals that are not domesticated, and we desire to have them protected. In North America, for instance, the deer population was at an all-time low around the 1900s, but through wise management it is now in substantially greater numbers than previously and there are no signs of their dying out. It is now obvious that most animal life and bird life on this continent can be preserved, and may even thrive, if man would only apply some relatively minor and modest measures of control. However, these are rather meagre.
A few years ago, when I first came to the House in 1968, I asked what research was available on upland game birds in the prairie provinces, Unfortunately, I found that very little research material was available and I was referred to research material accumulated by the Americans in the Dakotas and Montana. But even in that area the American research was quite meagre. For my own interest I was able
3584

May 9, 1973
Wildlife Protection
to procure some native varieties of seedling plantings for birds from the government station at Indian Head, and I believe that the government officials in the dominion nursery there have made a creditable start in this area. They are to be congratulated for having made a start in finding suitable plantings which will sustain game bird populations in the prairie area.
The problem with wildlife programs at both the federal and provincial levels has been the apparent lack of continuity of the programs once a project was under way. For instance, the government had a program of poghole preservation in western Manitoba which fell afoul of the government's austerity measures in 1969. The farmers at that time, since they had an excess of grain on hand, were glad to preserve some of the potholes for waterfowl preservation because of the income involved from the leasing; but at this time when grain is not so abundant-it is in short supply and it can all be sold-it will be more difficult to convince farmers to set them aside and leave them as a sluice for waterfowl preservation.
I would like to say that although the setting aside of selected areas as refuges has a good deal of advantage, I think that for the preservation of wildlife this should be done throughout the whole of the country, interspersed with farms, agricultural units, and so on. To do this we need the co-operation of the provincial and federal governments but, most importantly, we need the co-operation of rural councils. Speaking of my own area, there will not be much progress there unless the co-operation of rural councils is enlisted. Their help will have to be planned in the matter of restrictions, easements, perhaps direct tax relief measures, etc., which will have to be agreed upon in order that a suitable habitat for wildlife may be made available. It is quite true that a relatively small effort to maintain these habitats will be necessary to support a substantial wildlife population.
I am always amazed at the statement that the English countryside sustains a higher population of wild animals per square mile than any other country in the world. In Canada, and in the prairie provinces especially, with the severe winters wildlife population may not be extremely high but there is no doubt that with proper management surprisingly good results could be anticipated.
There is a problem in my area, which I think would be prevalent in many other areas, regarding hunting rights of the native people. Tensions are heightening between the Indian people and the rural communities surrounding reserves over the question of all-year hunting and what is considered a particularly unsportsmanlike method of hunting, night-lighting, by Indians on private property. Although Indians have a right to hunt during the year on reservations or on Crown land, there is actually little Crown land available, so that most hunting is done on private property. The original purpose of allow'ng Indians to hunt for food has long since lost its validity in the southern parts of the country, as all the game available could provide only a slight amount of food for the Indian population.
The double standard of having some people able to hunt all year round while others cannot hunt at all, particularly

when hunting is carried out on private land, has caused intense animosity in my area between the Indian people and the surrounding farm population and sportsmen. It is wisely pointed out that all the violations of night-lighting, and so on, are not caused by the Indians. Of course, the problem is complicated by the fact that the preservation of wildlife is under provincial jurisdiction. While the treaties which guarantee the Indians their right to hunt were made by the federal authority, up to the present time there has been no obvious attempt made by either the federal or provincial authorities to sort out this delicate problem.
It is a problem that will have to be solved. I urge the minister to have his department study this problem as well as having the Department of Indian Affairs study it so that meaningful discussions with the provinces and with the Indian bands themselves will lead to some kind of solution. Otherwise, I am afraid that the animosity may lead to violent solutions that we will all regret, and that will endanger the working out of satisfactory relationships between the Indians and their rural neighbours. This may not be a very widespread problem but it is a severe one. It goes to the root of the original treaties and also to the root of the enforcement of provincial game laws. I congratulate the minister on this bill and I wish its purpose success.

subtopic: CANADA WILDLIFE BILL
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR RESEARCH AND CONSERVATION AGREEMENTS, CONTRIBUTIONS TO COSTS AND PURCHASE, ACQUISITION OR LEASE OF LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to take part in the discussion on Bill C-131. Perhaps my initial observation will be similar to that of others who suggested that this is umbrella legislation. One of the problems with umbrella legislation is that it tends to be full of holes, in that it allows a minister to do a great deal or to do virtually nothing.
I realize that the problem of wildlife protection, management and enhancement in Canada is fraught with certain difficulties which are largely jurisdictional, and even with the best will in the world the federal government would have to seek the co-operation of provinces and municipalities before it could achieve its objectives. I also think that the matter of the regulations to flow from this bill is of major concern. Because of the very general nature of the bill, it seems to me that the regulations will determine whether or not Bill C-131 is to be effective or just window-dressing.
Without those regulations, or knowledge of them, we really cannot draw too many conclusions about this legislation, except that it is a statement of fine intentions. This is a continuing problem with a great deal of legislation presented to this House. I recall that a couple of years ago, when we were discussing the problem of protection of the boreal ecology with respect to the Yukon mineral bill, until we were sure which set of regulations would be accepted we in parliament were in a very poor position to make any intelligent comment on the nature, scope and possible effectiveness of that bill, and so with many other pieces of legislation. But in saying that, I think we can be pleased that we have this legislation before us, of course recognizing the limitations and also recognizing the fact that it is really up to the minister or the government to determine how much effect this will have in preserving and enhancing the kind of natural wildlife which abounds in Canada.
May 9, 1973

It is interesting, I think, that wildlife legislation took so long to arrive at the federal level. I believe it is here now because of a growing concern over and a recognition of the fact that we as men, as humans, are really "part of" rather than "apart from" the whole ecology of this planet. We have too long stood above the planet as its masters, but now we find that our mastery has not really been very masterful. We, like the animals, are part of the whole ecosystem, and man's transgressions are the most threatening to it.
About 20 years ago the standard text for general science in British Columbia was called "Mastering our Environment." I doubt whether a text with that title would ever find its way into the school system today because our whole attitude with respect to man's relationship to the environment has changed, perhaps due to the pioneering efforts of people such as Jack Miner dealing with birds, Grey Owl dealing with beavers and of writers who published interesting outdoor stories. Today more and more people are recognizing the validity of preserving the often limited and definitive parameters or boundaries of what survives in terms of wildlife, not only animal life but plant and marine life.
I do not intend to go into great detail in a clause by clause review of this bill. As I said earlier, I feel the bill is very general and that it is really up to the minister to determine what flows from it. Whether or not it is used to the benefit and preservation of wildlife really rests with the minister and his government. I would like to note-I will list some things in a moment and perhaps discuss them in detail later-some of the threats to wildlife which I think have brought us to the point where we must now consider this preservation legislation. The first thing we have to consider-and this is largely, by the way, centred around modern man-is the destruction that development of all kinds causes to wildlife. There is also the destruction of predators, which in turn destroys the food chain. There is the suffering and destruction due to the various kinds of savage traps that we use to catch animals. There is the destruction of animal life caused by chemical pollutants, herbicides, pesticides and various waste products. There is the destruction caused by government department ignoring another government department. I will amplify this later. Finally, the destruction of animals, both lethal and sublethal, having to do with the reproductive capacities of those animals, birds and fishes which is due to radioactive fall-out.
Mr. Speaker, it is rather pointless for us to be considering this legislation at all if we do not take a long strong stand on matters such as technological development, chemical and nuclear pollution and the ignorance of one government department compared to another. Unless we take all these things into consideration, we are only uttering a lot of fine sentiments and the result will be gradual extinction of more and more species. I have heard it said that we are losing one species of animal per year in the world. This figure is nothing for human beings to be proud of.
In British Columbia we have examples of destruction due to developments such as the Roberts Bank coal port. The bulk loading facility happened to be set in the only
Wildlife Protection
Mediterranean marine climate that exists in British Columbia. Many people opposed that port because of its situation within to marinetide flats and wetlands which is where the life of the sea starts. Any further depradation of this limited and unique Mediterranean marine area in Canada would be a definite loss not only for recreation but for those forms of marine and fish life that depend upon such areas to reproduce. This includes shellfish and other types of commercial fish.
I am pleased that now when we consider the construction of coal ports and such things as airports, we first embark upon environmental studies. I do not know how sophisticated these studies are, but at least greater consideration is being given to the environmental impact. No explicit references to environmental studies for annual protection before embarking on major developments are to be found in this bill. Another thing that concerns many B.C. people is the possibility that the mudflats east of the Second Narrows bridge on Burrard Inlet may be destroyed for the development of port facilities. I would oppose any such move because I believe we should try to preserve mudflats for the reasons I have mentioned in connection with Roberts Bank.
There have also been doubts about the development of the Mackenzie valley. I have in my file some material from the Canadian Wildlife Federation which came to me a couple of years ago when I was speaking about the Yukon Minerals Act. At that time we were as concerned about exploration and development by mining companies as we are today about the development of oil pipelines. In the winter, 1971, issue of Wildlife News appears the following comment:
Statements made recently in the House of Commons imply that the Canadian Wildlife Service is actively involved in research on the effects of pipelines on ecology in general and on wildlife in particular. Except for an inventory of sensitive wildlife areas, and a general reconnaissance of the types of damage being done by oil exploration-
And coming to the operative part of the statement, Mr. Speaker.
-the Canadian Wildlife Service has neither undertaken research of the type implied nor does it have funds for such research during the forthcoming year.
I hope the minister can tell us that is no longer true, or else everything contained in Bill C-131 is nonsense. Lack of funding reminds me of the Canada Water Act which was to provide the establishment of river basin boards. To my knowledge none has been set up, mainly because there was no provision for funds to cover them. It is all very well to have research into sensitive ecological matters, but if funds are denied we might as well forget the subject. There are some other interesting comments in the Wildlife Federation leaflet which bear not only on the attitudes of Canadians but also on North American or western European values. On page 2 appears the following:
But, as the Canadian Wildlife Federation points out in its current National Wildlife Week program, the earth is not without its limits-limits which we have known for several centuries. We have long since "conquered" the wilderness and "subdued" the last inhabitable frontiers. Our technology exploits forms of energy which gives to each of us power equivalent to hundreds of times the impact on our environment. The wastes and even the products of our rapidly growing, diversifying technology are too often released into the biosphere to upset the eons-old balance of natural systems.

May 9, 1973
Wildlife Protection
In other words, the Canadian Wildlife Service, a branch of government, is complaining that we are using the air as a sewer. We are. If we continue to do this it is bound to have a much more pernicious effect on our animal life than we can overcome by setting up any reserve for the resting of wild ducks. There exists the larger question which is important and one which goes beyond this legislation. I should like to read one more paragraph from this excellent bulletin because it relates to the larger question:
Clearly, our devotion to the growth ethos, the outmoded conventional wisdom that proclaims "bigger" to be "better", has been too complete for too long. Now that bigger populations, more products and by-products of technology, greater use of resources and proliferation of wastes are lowering the quality of our lives-perhaps even threatening our survival-it is surely time to make intelligent choices which, at best, may preserve a reasonable quality of life and, at worst, will avoid disaster for our species.
I think it is implied here that our species are inextricably linked with all other species on this planet. Perhaps I have said enough about that, but it reflects the attitude of many people and I am sure that in the main, though perhaps not completely, it reflects the attitude of the minister.
The next point is the destruction of predators which in turn destroy our food chain. For too long we have been chasing "the big bad wolf"-we allow the rodent to multiply, and so the whole ecosystem gets out of balance. A lady from my riding has written to me on this general topic and I should like to quote from her letter. She writes:
Our wildlife plays a vital part in our ecosystem-all wildlife- even the predators, that hunters and stockmen would have us believe are an "extra entity!" But then "self-interest" tends to make one's views a bit biased, wouldn't you say? Or to carry the thought further "man is the extra in the ecosystem!" He contributes little and feels justified in taking all he can get at the expense, in many instances, of the environment. The destruction of predators (so-called) is the irreversible first step toward destruction of land and the ecosystem. As the predators disappear, the rodents increase; as the rodents devour the roots of the grasses, the grass cover dies-causing erosion. With the destruction of the natural growth of grass cover, the so-called noxious plants take over-productive land becomes a desert!
From recent information we know that because of overgrazing, poor management practices and perhaps even a change in climate, the Sahara desert is growing by one mile per year and it could conceivably cover a huge portion of Africa in our lifetime. From our biblical studies we know, too, that the Holy Land was once a very lush and productive place but because of malpractice and lack of concern for environment we see what some areas have degenerated into.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I have said enough about the destruction of predators and how we have been blind to the necessity of maintaining a balanced ecosystem in our world. We can see what happens if you shoot the coyote, as the shooting of the coyote and his relatives meant that there were far more gophers who ate our grain and, consequently, caused a great deal of erosion, creating a potential wasteland where no life survives.
I should like to speak now for a moment about the destruction and suffering due to the savage and cruel trapping methods employed in Canada. I am not scorning those people, such as native peoples and others, who trap

for a living. What many do not know is that perhaps half the leg-hold traps are sold in urban areas are for catching pigeons, cats and other kinds of bothersome creatures around the city. It may be interesting to note that in the last few months there has been established an all-party, House of Commons animal welfare committee, the establishment of which was prompted by the efforts of Mr. Tom Hughes of the Animal Welfare Foundation. The committee has met once informally and will probably meet again. It is attempting to deal in a rational and reasonable way with the welfare of animals. At the moment the committee is chaired by my colleague, the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Mather) and, if it is successful in its endeavours, we hope that our work will lead to the development of a more healthy approach toward animals generally, and specifically help to stamp out the cruelty which is involved in the use of the leg-hold trap.
Especially since a number of grisly television documentaries on this subject were aired, interest in more human trapping methods has been growing. A class of school children from Port Coquitlam in my province wrote to me about this matter some weeks ago. They say:
We, the grade seven students of Irvine Elementary protest the use of leg-trapping of animals. Our class had a discussion on this subject and found there is another way such as the Conibear trap which kills instantly. Why couldn't the trappers use it?
The letter is signed by the students of that class. It seems to me that if students like those are beginning to realize what is happening, recognize the cruelty involved and display that sort of sensitivity and concern toward animals so that there may be safer and a more humane approach to their slaughter, if their slaughter is necessary, it bodes well for us, as does this legislation. After all, these children will be our future decision-makers.
This legislation is a reflection not only on the minister but on the times in which we live. I do not think the children are quite accurate in their assessment of traps. The Conibear trap, the supposed substitute for the leg-hold trap, does not meet all the necessary conditions entirely. It does not quite meet the ideal of being a perfect trap. I do not suggest that people who depend for their livelihood on the leg-hold trap should be denied its use until another one is developed, but the leg-hold trap should be sold to bona fide trappers only and kept out of the city.
Certainly, if there are to be grants and awards under this legislation the minister should consider, as a first priority, awarding grants for the development of a more humane kind of trap to be used on wild animals. A good place to start would be with the Conibear trap. In any event, whether it is important or not, I wanted to say it because many people whom I represent would want me to say it, as they are concerned about this subject.
I should like now to deal for a moment with the destruction caused by chemical pollutants such as the various herbicides, insecticides and various waste products that flow from our technological society. I reiterate, there is not much point in dealing with the lack of resting spots for the wild goose if we do not at the same time deal with pollutants. So long as we continue to pollute ourselves and our world, what is the point of a bill that encourages research into this and that, and will establish some sort of
May 9, 1973

resting place, in co-operation with the provinces, for geese? There is no point to it.
Take the matter of herbicides. We use phenoxy herbicides. Chemicals such as 24D, 245T, 245TP, Mecoprop, and so on, contain some of the chemical female hormones in addition to chlorinated hydrocarbons. Some of these chemicals have been around for years; others have been used most recently as defoliants in the Viet Nam war. Canada joined 58 other nations to secure the ban of these defoliants because they are dangerous, not just because they take leaves off trees in Viet Nam but because they are dangerous to humans and animals. Canada, along with 58 other nations of the United Nations asked for these chemicals to be banned. At the same time, although Canada has asked for these phenoxy herbicides to be banned in Viet Nam, our Canadian Department of Agriculture has authorized their use in Canada.
What do these chemicals do, Mr. Speaker? I am told that they are capable of causing bronchitis, myocardial damage, kidney and liver damage, neuritis, fatigue, depression, nervousness, headaches, disturbed sleep, attacks of giddiness, muscular aches and pains, edema, disturbances in memory, loss of weight, disturbances in concentration, uncontrollable bleeding involving the eyes, nose and other body openings and internal organs, cancer and deformed babies. The fumes can be as deadly when ingested. But, unbelievably, our Department of Agriculture authorizes the use of these chemicals in Canada.
If those chemicals used in Viet Nam are so thoroughly damaging to humans in the manner I have just outlined, what on earth will they do to animals? The damage caused by chemicals like these will far more than offset any benefit that may accrue to animals as a result of this legislation unless we are concurrently prepared to deal with that pollution. I hope the minister and his department will deal with them. Certainly, he ought to interest the Minister of Agriculture in reviewing his authorization of these chemicals. That is part of his job. If he does not do that, then this legislation is just so much tokenistic nonsense.
Consider for a moment what has happened in Texas. May I read an excerpt from a letter written by a lawyer in New Mexico who has this to say about the effects of certain chemicals:
Shortly after the spraying, the cattle of both of my clients began dying. The remaining cattle are emaciated and do not gain any weight although they are being fed in excess of the normal food ration. Calves have been aborted by mother cows; and, those calves that have been born alive since the spraying are only the size of large dogs.
If sprays can do that to domestic animals, what can they do to wild animals? The use of these chemicals has escalated because of continued tax-free pressure by the chemical lobby and various other lobbies. When we use these chemicals we remove one source of trouble and cause others. We are attempting to control one kind of horror with the use of another horror, and this will have to stop.
What about the case of the plastic waste in England which caused the shells of gulls' egg to become much thinner and severely limit reproductive capacity of these gulls? If these things continue to happen and We take no steps to control them, we shall be in great difficulty. What
Wildlife Protection
about the mercury in fish? What about pulp mill pollution in British Columbia? For years I have been trying to obtain from the minister his records of monitoring pulp mill effluent of the Fraser River, a very important part of our salmon resource, but with no success. And here the minister comes in with a bill that, as he says, will save the animals. It is difficult to reconcile those words with his past actions.
Also, let us consider the destruction caused by one department of government to wildlife as a result of ignoring the aims of another department of government. This week I received a request for an extension of a LIP project. That project is six weeks late. I suppose the LIP project could be made fun of and satirized. However, a number of people are devoted to building artificial nests around Pitt Lake for wood ducks an endangered species. Funds for the project came late and an extension was requested. If no extension is approved, the project will be eliminated or those involved will have to pay for it out of their own funds.
This is a case where the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis), in consultation with the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), who is in charge of I.IP funds, can make certain this project goes ahead. I am pleased to see the Minister of Manpower in his place because I have not yet made a personal representation to him on this subject. However, I have made representations to his department for an extension because this project deals with an endangered species. At the moment the project is in jeopardy, as is the species. One department of government must co-operate and communicate with the others. It is essential. Let me give another example which I mentioned earlier. Through the United Nations, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) asked for a ban on herbicides in Viet Nam. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) allows this same product to be used in Canada. That is a contradiction I find hard to reconcile.
There is another matter of interest. The Department of Transport authorized that a part of Pitt Meadows in my constituency be used as a helicopter practice range. This is precisely over the nesting area of an endangered species known as the sandhill crane. There are now only three or four pairs left in the area. When the sandhill crane is nesting, the helicopters disturb them and they fly away from their nests.
The concluding item on my list of destruction of wild animals and wildlife in general is the destruction caused by radioactive fall-out. There are both lethal and sublethal effects. I do not think anyone realizes the extent of genetic damage caused by this. This is one reason why since coming to this House I have been doing everything I can to discourage the obscenities of further nuclear testing whether underground or on the water. I do not think people realize the amount of radiation pollution we have been ingesting since World War II. I have a paper which was prepared by Professor Gordon Edwards, department of mathematics, University of British Columbia. I will read from it briefly. I would like to make it as interesting as possible, which is a difficult thing when quoting. It reads;

May 9, 1973
Wildlife Protection
During the atmospheric testing of the 1950s, the AEC predicted (correctly) that much less fallout would reach the ground in arctic regions than in temporate regions of the United States. They concluded (incorrectly) that Eskimos would not be in danger of accumulating dangerous amounts of fallout. They didn't know that food chains can behave in peculiar ways. Lichens . . . have no functional roots, and often grow on rocks rather than soil. They absorb their mineral nutrition in the form of dust taken directly from the air. As a result they absorb radioactive fallout directly, without the dilution and discrimination processes which operate when fallout is absorbed through roots. Caribou eat great quantities of lichen (many times their own body weight) and therefore take up excessive amounts of radiation from fallout. At the end of the food chain, caribou meat makes up a substantive portion of the Eskimo's diet, producing the unexpectedly large amounts of fallout radiation in their bodies.
This is not only true in the Arctic. It applies to milk and other products. There are dozens of other examples. If radiation is a threat to humans, it naturally follows that there exists a threat to animals. The government has to move in the direction to grapple effectively with radiation. Unless they do, the sentiments expressed in this piece of legislation will fall far short of reality.
Someone called this a motherhood bill. I think that is a bit cruel. Bill C-131 at least recognizes the problem of endangered species and does so for the first time. In British Columbia some wags may take the term "endangered species" to mean the Liberal party. Nevertheless, my party intends to support this bill. The bill, however, makes little mention of the points I have raised and seems to be deficient in explicit power to prevent abuses. Before setting down I also would like to congratulate the rod and gun clubs as well as groups such as SPEC and the Coquitlam River Committee for bringing the nature of the problems directly to the attention of legislators. Without the private interest groups and environmental groups there would certainly have been less motivation to have wildlife legislation considered during this session.
I will try not to be cynical, but I wonder what impact this bill will have on the massive environmental rape known as the James Bay project. How will this bill protect the animals in that area? If the minister will excuse me for accusing him for being a bit lethargic on the matter of the Skagit, I wonder how it would have helped the animals in the Skagit valley. How would this bill have helped predict the difficulties associated with the Bennett Dam in the Athabasca basin?
These are extremely important matters since wildlife protection does not deal with single issues. They are broad and comprehensive. They are not just limited to wildlife. Our reactions are determined by the attitudes and traditions we have. It is about time we changed some of them. I do not want to appear unduly sanctimonous, but we are all products of the habits of how we have been raised. Talking and reading about new attitudes and new realities is how they gain general acceptance.
In conclusion, possibly the House might consider the private member's bill of my colleague, the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Harney), Bill C-165 which, as he stated, broadens the definition of "endangered species." With the minister's co-operation, possibly Bill C-185 might be sent to the committee at the same time as Bill C-131.
I am pleased to have had the opportunity to speak on this bill. I congratulate the minister for bringing it forward. I hope some real action will flow from it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate that has resulted from the presentation of Bill C-131 has been largely a ritualistic exercise. I do not think anyone is going to oppose this bill because the principles it espouses, the wise management and possible use of renewable resources, has long been accepted by the federal government, provincial governments, municipal governments and the people of Canada. Indeed, I feel that the people of Canada are ahead of governments in this regard. It is only by continuing pressure that we now have harmonized in the bill before the House these principles vital to the preservation and conservation of our renewable resources.
My contribution this afternoon will be brief. I do not intend to outline a grandiose policy of wildlife management. I do wish, however, to pay tribute to some of the pioneers whose efforts have made this bill possible. We have just come through National Wildlife Week which occurs annually during the early part of April. I am sure all members will be aware that it is a tribute to the pioneering work of Jack Miner who founded one of the first migratory wildfowl sanctuaries in the southern part of Ontario. This parliament eventually recognized the pioneering work of the Miner sanctuary and passed legislation which made the annual observance possible.
In addition, I should like to refer to the Resources for Tomorrow Conference of 1961 which I think was a high-water mark in the emergence of the legislation now before the House. As the minister told us in his opening remarks, one of the resolutions which came out of that conference urged upon governments, particularly at the provincial and federal levels, the passing of wildlife legislation which would attempt to deal with problems which had already been defined. One of the pioneers in this effort was the Canadian Wildlife Service itself. Canada has been well served by this branch of government and some of the men who have served as directors of the department over the years must be mentioned as largely responsible for the legislation before us today. I shall not mention any names. I shall simply indicate that during the past two or three decades the directors of that department have called attention in season and out of season to the necessity for legislative action to ensure that wildlife, as part of our renewable resources, is wisely managed.
The Resources for Tomorrow Conference also led to the establishment of a resource ministers' council. It is my opinion that there is lack of appreciation of the role this council has played and can play in its important responsibility of co-ordinating wise management measures in all areas affecting renewable resources. For example, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding), speaking in the debate last night, as reported at page 3543 of Hansard, referred to the effort which he says he has made many times in the House to bring about the establishment of an environmental council wholly independent of government and entrusted with reporting on environmental problems throughout the country.
Mr. Speaker, we already have such a council-the resource ministers' council which brings together annually, and more frequently if necessary, all the provincial ministers across the country in council with the federal
May 9, 1973_________________COMMONS DEBATES_______________________ 3589
minister so that they may achieve some measure of coordination in an area where it is most difficult to achieve co-operation because of the constitutional jurisdictional problem. The headquarters of the council were deliberately established outside the city of Ottawa so there would be no suspicion of any direct connection with government at any level. The council operates out of Montreal. It has a highly qualified secretariat and its function is to do exactly what the hon. member for Kootenay West is apparently advocating.
So the council already exists, and the fact that a Member of Parliament is not aware of it indicates that it has hardly been given the prominence that its important responsibilities deserve. It was in 1965 that this council passed a resolution reinforcing the resolution which came out of the Resources for Tomorrow Conference of 1961 urging legislative action to carry out the responsibilities of wise management of Canadian wildlife resources. We should pay tribute here this afternoon to those who have pioneered in the resources ministers' council and who perhaps have not received the measure of support which the importance of their work merits and who, in particular, have not received the financial support necessary if we are to achieve positive results under this program.
Another emanation of the Resources for Tomorrow Conference was the Canadian Wildlife Federation. That body was born from the conference. It was hailed at the time as one of the important achievements of the conference. The federation brought together the fish and game associations across the country and it has, I believe, been one of the major influences in urging governments at all levels to act in making possible the production of the legislation now before the House.
We all realize that legislation of itself will not achieve positive results unless there is initiative and action on the part of all governments. This follows from the jurisdictional problem to which I have already referred, one which makes it extremely difficult if not impossible to get action in the area of policies affecting conservation. The hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose), who spoke just before me, outlined programs and policies which he said might be activated by the federal government. The federal government can activate nothing unless it gets the co-operation of the provinces, hence the importance of the resource ministers' council. I feel the provinces are ahead of the federal government in this regard.
I am reminded, for example, that the resource minister for Quebec who served on a committee of the Resources for Tomorrow Conference in 1961 was a politician by the name of Rene Levesque. Perhaps he might have become more closely associated with matters of national unity had there not been so much delay in implementing the resolution of the Resources for Tomorrow Conference in this respect.

Mr. Levesque objected to the presence of a federal minister-perhaps there were some separatist sentiments evident in that regard-presiding over the steering committee since Ottawa did not have jurisdiction over renewable resources. When I was chairman I indicated that I was also functioning as minister of northern affairs. He shrugged in his inimitable fashion and said I could continue as minister of northern affairs since Ottawa had jurisdiction, but not as minister of resources. This was a diversionary tactic which must always be exercised when it comes to dealing with the provinces in these matters if positive results are going to be achieved.
We now have legislation that all hon. members who have spoken this afternoon have concurred is long overdue. It is merely enabling. Nothing will happen unless funds are available. And here is where the crunch comes. I think that if Ottawa is going to make the legislation effective, in positive terms it must indicate what its funding priorities are. I have already intimated that the vitally important resource ministers' council has been inhibited and hampered in its work because adequate funds have not been available. As already mentioned here this afternoon, it is significant that one of the programs that fell under the measure of austerity of 1969 was the excellent pothole leasing project. It was very difficult in the first instance to get farmers to co-operate in leasing land to preserve the potholes of the Prairies where most of the duck population is generated, and I think it was a retrograde step of some proportion for Ottawa arbitrarily to cancel a program of this kind just when it was receiving ready acceptance from the prairie farmers.
I hope that programs such as this will be restored and enlarged upon, because it is this kind of leadership in the field of federal funding that is going to ensure the effectiveness of the act and the continuing co-operation of the provincial governments. One of the hopeful aspects of the wholly new attitude toward wise management and multiple use of renewable resources is the leadership being provided by young people. I think the generation that is now coming upon the scene will be much more positive than that which is gradually leaving the scene of action.
When we get this bill into committee I hope, since some members have suggested that the bill needs strengthening, we might give some attention to replacing some of the "mays" with "shalls", always of course being aware, as the bill is aware, that provincial agreement must be reached in

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to join other members in welcoming Bill C-131. The bill will provide for a program of rehabilitation, habitat preservation and research for rare and endangered species within Canada. I am disappointed, though, that the bill does not include some provision for prohibiting entry into Canada of species of animals that are endangered throughout the world. I realize the rationale behind not doing so. There is a convention presently being drafted by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources, and I understand we are waiting for the completion of this convention before preparing legislation which, in a sense, will be complementary to Bill C-131 and will deal with the importation of endangered species into Canada.
In the meantime, however, things are going on which are contributing to the continuing decline in population of a wide range of species of animals and reptiles. If allowed to continue for another year or two at its present rate, these species will be pushed past the point of no return, and certainly into extinction within five or six years. It seems to me that we could by order in council now take certain measures that could contribute, at least as far as Canada is concerned, to stopping the drain on these irreplaceable species of wildlife.
I have had a bill before the House of Commons for three sessions now relating to the protection of endangered species of animals. The object of the bill that I have introduced-its present label is Bill C-88-is to protect species of animals and also birds, amphibians, reptiles, mollusks and crustaceans which are in danger of extinction. The bill would do this whether they are endangered on a worldwide basis or on a local habitat basis, and this is an improvement over a couple of earlier bills. It is very important that we make this distinction because some species, although they may not be endangered on a local basis are in danger of elimination from even one hemisphere or another, and any legislation or order in council we have here in Canada must take this into consideration.
To achieve the objective of protecting these species in danger of extinction, the bill which I propose would prohibit the importation into Canada of not only the furs, skins, etc., of these species but any part thereof or any product manufactured from a part thereof. This would include a cosmetic product that was manufactured from the oil of an endangered species of whale and it would include perhaps costume jewellery manufactured from endangered species of molluscs, etc.
This would go much further, in my view, than we are likely to see in any convention which is presently being drafted by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and National Resources. I have been in touch with our customs people who have been studying the matter, and I gather from talking with our own customs officials

that it would be possible for the Canadian government to now or very quickly enforce restrictions under schedule C of the Customs Tariff. I understand this has been discussed with the national body drawing up the convention, but I gather that the body drawing up the convention is concentrating on sources of exports rather than on imports. Because of the world trend today toward simplifying procedures of customs varification through spot checks, it just does not make practical, common sense to try to do very much about imports. I take issue with this and I think they are seriously underestimating the strength of public opinion in this regard.
I would urge strongly that Canada take steps on its own through an order in council to prohibit the importation of all endangered species or parts thereof. I would suggest that even though we may have customs spot checks, as we now have, that arouse public opinion, hon. members of this House could find very many groups in their ridings who would go out policing to make sure that any endangered species of animals which appears on any store counter, or any cosmetic sold in any drugstore which contains a part of an endangered species, a whale for example, would be brought to the attention of the competent authorities. I feel that public opinion would provide much more effective policing than any customs check we could develop. We need not kid ourselves that customs could handle this completely, effectively or in an airtight way, but we do not have to depend on customs. Let us get the law on the books and we will leave it up to the public and the various environmental groups which exist in this country to enforce it; and I am convinced they can.
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister- he may already be aware of it-a very serious abuse that has occurred within the last month and a half because we do not have any import regulations of this kind in Canada. The state of New York in particular, as well as the United States in general, have a very tough endangered species act which prohibits the importation into the United States of skins, furs, etc. Approximately six weeks ago a very important shipment of illicit skins from South America came into Canada and was exported to the United States, circumventing the U.S. customs officials. Through some very effective detective work this circumvention was discovered. These illicit traders are using Canada right now as a means to circumvent the severe import restrictions which exist in the United States.
I feel strongly that we should be taking steps now-and we could through an order in council-to prohibit absolutely the importation into Canada of these endangered species. We could bring this regulation in now, and when the international convention is in final form and we approve it by legislation, that could take the place of whatever order in council or regulation we may have enacted.
I hope the minister will be receptive to the suggestion of having at least the substance contained in both the private member's bill submitted by the hon. member for Scarborough West, Bill C-165, and my Bill C-88 referred to the committee which will be considering Bill C-131. I do not ask, necessarily, that the bills themselves be referred to the committee, but if we could have the subject matter referred by unanimous consent it would be useful. We
May 9, 1973

could perhaps bring in a number of witnesses to give their opinion as to precisely the most effective type of measure we could adopt here in Canada to contribute to the cessation of this illicit trade in endangered species or parts thereof.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in the debate on Bill C-131 relating to wildlife services in Canada because of the very direct application it has to the area I represent, namely, the county of Norfolk. The Wildlife Service has only recently purchased a marsh in the area of Long Point from the Big Creek Company, and is presently making a survey of the area for the purpose of administering it to the best advantage of the people of the area and the wildlife which inhabit the marsh.
Let me refer specifically to clauses 3(a) and 3(e) wherein the word "co-operation" appears twice. It refers to the co-operation in wildlife and interpretation thereof and co-operation with the government of the province having an interest. In this particular instance, side by side with that area of the marsh acquired by the Wildlife Service is another area formerly owned by a local resident, Mr. Lee M. Brown, a very ardent conservationalist, comprising about 60 acres. This was recently given to the Long Point conservation authority which administers conservation activities throughout Norfolk and Haldimand counties. This provides an excellent opportunity for the co-operation which is mentioned twice in the bill.
I bring this to the attention of the minister and members of the House because I feel a very grave injustice has been done to Mr. Brown, the conservationalist to whom I referred, in that he was found guilty and fined in a local magistrate's court for contravention of the Migratory Birds Convention Act. Mr. Brown, as I said, has been a lifelong conservationist and is recognized throughout the area as such. He built up a sanctuary for Canada geese there, rivalling in a small way Jack Miner's sanctuary already referred to by the hon. member for Brandon-Sou-ris (Mr. Dinsdale). Crowds are flocking there to see wild geese during the migratory bird season.
I referred to the injustice done to this man, and I think it is best illustrated in a letter written to the editor of the Simcoe Reformer of Tuesday, April 17, part of which I would like to read into the record. It is written by a former editor of that paper, a lifelong resident of Norfolk and a friend of Mr. Brown. This is what he said in part:
In any case it seems a strange reward to Lee M. Brown for his generous act in deeding the sanctuary and about 60 acres of surrounding property free of charge to the conservation authority. His conviction and the levying of a fine against him is surely a peculiar way to express gratitude to one of Norfolk's leading conservationists and a man who has given many years of his life to building up a sanctuary for Canada geese and other bird life and who has expended many thousands of dollars of his own resources in feeding the thousands of birds and otherwise caring for them-
I will conclude with the following paragraph:
Now the outcome of this court case must give Mr. Brown occasion to wonder at such an expression of public gratitude for his unremitting work over the years in providing a haven of a unique character for birdlife in the Long Point area. Certainly he
Wildlife Protection
had good reason for discouragement in carrying out any further plans of this kind or to turn over more property to an ungrateful officialdom.
His many friends will resent the injustice done to one of Norfolk's most devoted conservationists.
I knew that this case was coming up so I wrote to the Wildlife Service here. Some of the men in the service are personal friends of Mr. Brown. I thought that in light of what I have already stated it would be only fair and just that this action against him be withdrawn. After all, there is the spirit of the law as well as the letter of the law to observe. I refer again to the co-operation which I trust the legislation proposed in Bill C-131 will bring about among men like Mr. Brown, the Long Point conservation authority under the provincial government, and the Wildlife Service of Canada, and prevent such an incident from ever happening again.
All Mr. Brown was doing was thinning out the male population of blue billed ducks in that area at the time of the mating season, because often they would destroy the nests, kill the females and prevent the proper incubation of eggs. For this act he was technically and legally found guilty and was fined. But, after all, the spirit of the act should be applied as well as the letter of the law. We admit that justice must be done but, most important of all, justice must be seen to be done-and this certainly was not the case with respect to Mr. Brown.
So in supporting this legislation, as we all do, I appeal to the minister to ensure that when the regulations under the act are drawn up and the act is administered, there be some spirit of understanding and of humanity toward those people who are already doing great work in the field of conservation which this bill proposes to assist and increase.
There is more I could say, Mr. Speaker, but I know other hon. members wish to make a contribution to this debate and therefore I will close my remarks.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also want to join my colleagues in supporting Bill C-131 and the principles and objectives contained therein. It is encouraging to note that the bill authorizes the minister to promote wildlife conservation, engage in various research activities and establish the entering into of agreements with advisory committees, the provinces, municipalities and individual persons.
However, my purpose in entering the debate is specifically to point out what I consider to be a grave injustice done to many farmers in western Canada, particularly those who are located adjacent to bird sanctuaries in areas where waterfowl make their habitat. It is rather disturbing to note that there is nothing in the bill to provide for what I consider to be the basic ingredient in the maintenance of our wildlife, namely, food. For many years ducks and geese have been sponging off the farmer, to his financial and economic detriment and I believe that a great injustice is being done to the farmers directly affected.
It is no great secret that the wildlife of which we are all proud is a natural asset enjoyed by all people. However, I do not believe that the burden of maintaining ducks, geese and waterfowl which migrate should fall totally on the farmers. Millions of dollars worth of damage has been

May 9, 1973
Wildlife Protection
done throughout the years and very little constructive effort has been made to compensate farmers for their losses.
In my own constituency of Vegreville there are two bird sanctuaries, the Beaver Hill sanctuary and the Whitford Lake sanctuary. I believe it is reasonable to assume that the wildlife there is the property of the Canadian people and therefore it should be up to the Canadian people to contribute to its maintenance. I think that the damage done by waterfowl is described very specifically in a booklet that has been put out by the Western Canadian Wildlife Advisory Committee, entitled "Uninvited Guests". To many producers in western Canada, ducks and geese, particularly in the wet fall season, are truly uninvited guests.
In the province of Alberta a fund has been established by the sportsmen of the province for the purpose of defraying some of the losses that the farmers have suffered. This fund was reimbursing $15 per acre over the years, but because of the heavy drain on it this amount has been adjusted to 86.15 per cent of $15, which works out to $12 or $12.50 per acre. I have a claims settlement sheet which was issued to a farmer in my constituency, a gentleman by the name of George Kucher who had 55 acres of barley totally damaged. It was inspected by the inspector of the Alberta hail and crop insurance board. To compensate him for his 100 per cent loss he received $710.74. That is a far cry from what he could have received had he been able to harvest this crop, which was barley. Fifty-five acres of barley would produce roughly $40 to $45 an acre. A reasonable estimate would be $40 an acre, and it would result in this producer obtaining some $2,200 out of his 55 acres of barley. However, because of the damage done by ducks he had to settle for some $710.74.
He lost another 85 acres in the same manner and received $1,098 to cover his loss-a far cry from what he could have received had he been able to harvest the crop. It seems to me that this particular gentleman, as well as many others who are trying to make a living from their efforts at farming, should be entitled to more adequate compensation than they have received, and I believe the federal government and the provincial governments should share the burden.
There are many ways in which this could be done. Perhaps a more effective lure program could be provided. But in addition to the loss which is sustained, each time a producer has to have an inspection it costs him $25 to have an inspector come from the Alberta hail insurance board to inspect his crop. In a particularly wet year he may end up having two or three inspections, depending on the length of time the harvest takes. In this particular case, in the crop year of 1971 Mr. Kucher had to pay out something like $75 for three different inspections made by an inspector of the Alberta hail insurance board.
I do not want to prolong this debate. I simply say to the minister that I hope some mechanism will be provided whereby adequate compensation will be made available to people who are afflicted by loss of crops due to damage by migratory waterfowl. I believe that the payment of $15 per acre is totally insufficient. It should be something in the

order of $35 to $40. I believe that the fee of $25 per inspection should be abolished. I also believe more sufficient lure crops and more adequate arrangements for areas situated close to bird sanctuaries should be provided so that losses would not be sustained year after year. Wet years are not uncommon in Canada and losses can occur year after year.
I hope that the minister, in co-operation with the provincial governments and municipalities, will be able to arrive at a suitable arrangement so that these people may be better compensated, thus creating a much greater understanding between those who support our wildlife by providing food and those who enjoy the advantages of our wildlife.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by saying, on behalf of all my colleagues, that we welcome this piece of legislation and I congratulate the minister for bringing it before the House. It has been said that it is a decade or so late, but better late than never. I think it is, or can be a useful piece of legislation.
The second thing I would like to say is in connection with the remarks of the two hon. members who have introduced bills which deal with the abolition of the trade in the pelts and skins of endangered species. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I wish to convey to both of these colleagues, who are on different sides of the House, the fact that they will have my absolute support in bringing their bills forward and I will do everything within my power to expedite the passage of those bills. Having said that, perhaps some discussion might take place afterward so that this can be achieved.
Having said some nice things, I now want to ask all members of the government side of the House to pay attention for just a few minutes while I say something that I believe they should hear. Let there be no mistake about it, Mr. Speaker; this bill does not do very much more than has been done in practice in the past. Secondly, I am concerned, and I think all hon. members ought to be concerned, that apparently the minister is treating the federal jurisdiction north of 60 degrees, so far as the problem of initiating action under this bill is concerned, as though he were dealing with provinces. I remind all hon. members of the government side that that area comprises 44 per cent of the land mass of Canada and over that 44 per cent we do have federal jurisdiction.
Please let us not back away from the authority we have when we are dealing with a matter which is becoming as vital as the preservation of our wildlife, something which we are now starting to recognize is not an inexhaustible resource, something which is a priceless resource. From the speeches made today it can be seen that we all agree about this. I beg hon. members on the government side to take this message back to their colleagues. Do not back out of an area of jurisdiction and the authority you already have, since this bill can be so useful in that area even if it has its difficulties elsewhere.

Ottawa, Ontario, K1A 0K9.
April 18th, 1973.
My dear Minister,
Re: New Financing Arrangements In The Health Care Field
As you will recall, a revised federal proposal for new financing arrangements in the health care field was presented to the Joint Meeting of Ministers of Health and the Federal/Provincial Committee of Ministers of Finance and Provincial Treasurers on January 19, 1973. Provincial ministers at the time were asked to study the revised proposal with a view to reconvening with us in about two months' time for the purpose of trying to reach agreement on the amount of the federal contribution for health services. Telegrams were recently sent to all provincial ministers concerned advising that this further meeting will take place on May 8 and 9.
In the discussion immediately following presentation of the revised federal offer, provincial ministers commented on the financial features of the proposal. They stated their concern about the adequacy of the escalator and questioned whether the newly introduced risk-sharing feature would provide sufficient protection should there be unexpected escalation in costs at a rate in excess of the escalation in the federal contribution. Subsequently, in the
course of the technical discussions which took place after January 19 officials of several provinces likewise raised these two issues and elaborated on the reasons for their being a cause of concern. A criticism of the proposed risk-sharing formula related to its non-cumulative characteristics, i.e., it made no provision for repeating in subsequent years any federal contribution in respect of excess escalation in costs that a province might experience in a particular year. There was, of course, a reason for this. In relation to long term cost projections for hospital and medical services and the improved effectiveness which provinces should be able to achieve in providing health services as a result of being able to use the federal contribution throughout the entire range of services, the federal government considered that its contributions under its previous proposal would be adequate. The availability of a large block of thrust funds to assist provinces to develop and introduce more economical methods of delivering services provided further support for this view.
Notwithstanding the above considerations the federal government now has further reviewed these two aspects of the proposal and taking into account the possibility of provinces encountering unexpected situations, has approved further modifications as follows:
(a) The declining 1 per cent adjustment incorporated in the escalator to be advanced from 1974-75 to 1973-74. The following illustrates how the escalator now proposed compares with the one contained in the January 19 proposal:
