The base year would continue to be 1972/73 with present arrangements maintained in 1973/74 and thrust funds made available in that year. However, it is necessary to escalate the 1972/73 federal per capita contributions to provinces pursuant to the formula through 1973/74 in order to determine the 1974/75 per capita contributions. You will appreciate that improving the escalator in 1973/74 by advancing the declining 1 per cent has a significant effect on the level of the per capitas, and consequently on the gross contributions in the years thereafter. In particular, it creates a rate of escalation in the federal contribution that matches more closely the rate of escalation in the estimated provincial costs during the early years of the new arrangements.
(b) The risk-sharing formula to be cumulative but on a diminishing basis. In this way, the federal government
would be able to take account of certain important provincial concerns, but'without abandoning the fundamental objectives of the new financing formula.
Under this approach risk-sharing payments made in a particular year under the "75-50-25" formula contained in the January proposal would be phased out in subsequent years in the following manner:
-a risk-sharing contribution made in the first year, i.e. 1974/75, would be followed by payments equal to 3/4, 1/2 and 1/4 of that contribution in the second, third and fourth years respectively;
-a further risk-sharing contribution or one made for the first time in the second year, i.e., 1975/76, would be followed by payments equal to 2/3 and 1/3 of that contribution in the third and fourth years respectively;
May 9, 19V3

a similar type of contribution made in the third year would be followed with a payment equal to one-half of that contribution in the fourth year;
-contributions towards excess expenditures in the fourth (1977/78) and fifth (1978/79) years of a new health financing agreement would not be followed by additional payments in subsequent years.
(Note: An illustration of this revised approach is contained in the attached folder).
This modified risk-sharing feature recognizes that excess expenditures i.e., the value of the difference between the rate of escalation in the federal contribution and provincial costs, incurred in a year might recur in whole or in part in succeeding years. This revised approach would relieve the provinces of a portion of the additional financial burden accruing to the provinces in succeeding years as a result of unexpected additional expense in one year. The principle of phasing out risksharing payments recognizes that, if a province spends at a rate that exceeds federal contributions in a year, such a province should be able, through economies in other parts of its health program, gradually to de-escalate costs to its original target rate of expenditure. Furthermore, the revised risk-sharing provisions assume that provincial administrations, with the use of thrust funds, will be in a better position to prevent excess expenditures by the last few years of the proposed new arrangements.
Finally, in assessing this revised proposal, provincial ministers no doubt will recall that federal contributions under the risk-sharing formula will be in relation to total health expenditures as defined.
Another issue briefly raised at the January 19 conference and further discussed in the subsequent technical meetings related to the loss of federal contributions under the Canada Assistance Plan that occur when a province changes the basis for its support to health or health related services (such as nursing home care) from a needstest basis to an insured or universal basis. A policy that results in the loss of CAP contributions when a province introduces changes of this nature in the health services field might be inconsistent with the basic objectives of the federal proposal for new financing arrangements. Accordingly, the federal government is prepared to agree that where a province participating under the new arrangements chooses, or has chosen, to make available health or health-related benefits on a universal basis in an area in which there has been federal cost-sharing under the Canada Assistance Plan, that province will be entitled to receive similar levels of federal financial contributions as it would have received had it not introduced the universal program. You will appreciate that this is a rather complex subject and, consequently, the mechanism for implementing this principle has to be worked out jointly. I will be prepared to explore with my provincial counterparts alternative methods for its implementation.
With these additional modifications, I believe the federal proposal now provides a full and reasoned response to the principal concerns which certain provincial governments have enunciated respecting the proposed new health financing agreement.
As for the form of the federal contribution, a number of provinces have suggested that this should be by way of a transfer of tax room. If the newly revised proposal on the quantum contained in this letter is accepted by provincial governments, the federal Minister of Finance remains ready to discuss in detail, at our meeting of May 8-9, the possibility of some transfer of tax room. In this regard I am attaching a copy of a separate letter that Mr. Turner has written to his provincial counterparts.
I am also attaching folders which contain new calculations reflecting the latest cost projections that we have received from the province, recent revisions to our assumptions concerning the future performance of the gross national product and the modification in the escalator described on page 2 of this letter. You will note that on the basis of the assumptions made with respect to future health cost trends of your province and the GNP rate of growth, it is calculated that the basic federal contribution to your province (i.e., excluding the risk-sharing provision) under the proposed new arrangements compares favourably with the estimated contribution that would be made if present arrangements were retained. These figures exclude the additional contributions that would be available should it become necessary to invoke the risksharing formula.
You may recall that some months ago I forwarded to you in mimeograph form copies of Dr. A.P. Ruderman's report which formed an appendix to the Report on Community Health Centres prepared by the committee under the chairmanship of Dr. John Hastings. Dr. Ruderman's report now has been printed in final form and I am pleased to forward two copies of it to you.
I look forward to renewing our discussion on the very important subject of new financing arrangements in the health care field, and I hope that this new proposal will meet with your approval and enable us to finalize the matter very soon.
Yours truly,
Marc Lalonde.

You will recall that the Prime Minister wrote to provincial First Ministers on November 9, 1970, suggesting that the post-secondary education fiscal transfer program be extended for two years, in order to provide time for a review of the present arrangements. Following further discussions between my predecessor, the Honourable Gerard Pelletier, and the Council of Ministers of Education, as well as with individual Ministers of Education, it was decided that the 1967 program should continue until March 31, 1974, with a national rate of growth in the federal contribution not exceeding 15 per cent per annum.
The present program of fiscal transfers in support of post-secondary education will therefore have been in operation for seven years when it expires on March 31, 1974. It may be useful, in light of the examination which we have carried out since that time, and of comments of other interested governments, if I were to review briefly a
May 9, 1973

few of the major considerations relating to the development of the program to date.
First, it is significant to note that annual operating expenditures have risen at a rapid rate during the life of the program, especially in the early years when for example the percentage increases were of the order of 25 per cent between 1967-68 and 1968-69, although they declined thereafter to an estimated 7.9 per cent between 1972-73 and 1973-74. It is also noteworthy that, in line with this growth pattern, federal contributions increased substantially in each succeeding year of the program and that the value of transfers to the provinces in respect of postsecondary education will have reached an estimated cumulative total of some $5.3 billion by March 1974, as indicated on an annual basis in table 1.
With the assistance of these transfers the provinces and the institutions were able to set in motion an unprecedented expansion of post-secondary instruction. As shown in table 2, the number of full-time students in universities and colleges and other post-secondary institutions across Canada increased during the first five years of the program by 60 per cent to a total of 497,000. In addition to full-time students, an estimated 250,000 persons were attending post-secondary institutions in Canada on a parttime basis in the fifth year of the program and costs relating to a further 200,000 at the senior matriculation level were also eligible for federal contributions under the program.
A number of demographic factors have also been and will continue to be of major importance. Of particular relevance is the size of the 18-24 age group which up to now has been the source of more than 80 per cent of all full-time post-secondary enrolments. When the present fiscal transfer program went into effect the ranks of Canadians in the 18-24 age group were growing at a record-breaking pace, and by 1971 their number had reached 2.7 million, an increase of 552,000 over a five-year period. As shown in table 3, however, the rate of growth of this age group will be progressively slower in the present decade until approximately 1983 when the number of 18-24 year olds will begin to decline in absolute terms.
The above-mentioned factors indicate, I believe, that the present program was established in 1967 to respond to a very special set of circumstances in the post-secondary education sector, Furthermore, in our view, the program has on the whole been successful in meeting the objectives which were foremost in the governments' minds in 1966. At the same time, we are of course aware that there may have been certain shortcomings in the existing arrangements and that from time to time the program has been the subject of criticism by provincial governments. For example, some provinces are of the opinion that the arrangements have represented a pressure on their priorities and that unavoidable rigidities inherent in the formula may to some degree have inhibited innovation and adaptation of educational structures to changing needs. We are also aware that the program may have permitted certain inequities, in that it allows those provinces in which the greatest amounts are spent to claim the largest federal transfers.
In the circumstances, the federal government has given careful attention, in the course of its review, to ways and means of removing these shortcomings and of introducing improvements which would result in a more satisfactory arrangement from both the provincial and federal points of view. In particular, we have examined a number of alternative financing formulae which might assist in meeting more adequately the generally accepted objectives of interregional and interpersonal equity.
At the same time, we are aware of and accept the continued importance of adequate financing of postsecondary education in Canada and believe that funding should continue at a level which will enable governments to meet their obligations in this sector. As a result, the federal government considers it of prime importance to provide a level of contributions which will ensure that the needs of the provinces can be adequately met on both a medium- and long-term basis.
In light of all the above considerations I should like to propose to provincial governments a conversion of the present program of fiscal transfers into a system of provincial per capita entitlements based on the size of the 18-24 age group in each province and escalated at 7 percent per annum, subject to a levelling provision designed to bring all provincial per capita entitlements to parity over a ten-year period. Such entitlements would continue to be met through a combination of the present tax points relating to post-secondary education and adjustment payments, and the conversion formula would be in effect for five years commencing April 1, 1974.
The formula would be based on eligible actual operating expenditures for the fiscal year 1973-74 calculated according to part VI of the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act, 1972. Table 3 indicates that, on the basis of current estimates it is likely that the fiscal transfer will amount in that year to approximately $1,066 million. Table 4 illustrates the estimated entitlement for each province for the year 1974-75 and for each of the four subsequent years. According to our present calculations, an escalator of 7 per cent per annum multiplied by the population 18-24 will produce an average national annual increase in the federal contributions during the next five years of some 9.4 per cent as compared with the latest estimate of a 7.9 increase in eligible operating expenditures on post-secondary education between 1972-73 and
1973-74.
I hope the above proposals will be satisfactory to all provincial governments and I look forward to hearing your reaction at the Federal-Provincial Conference of Ministers of Finance, Health and Education on May 8 and 9. I understand that the question of the post-secondary education fiscal transfer will be dealt with on May 8 in the afternoon.
Yours sincerely,
J. Hugh Faulkner

subtopic: FINANCING THE FEDERAL SHARE OF HEALTH SERVICES

speechtext:
Notes for Remarks by Finance Minister John N. Turner to a Joint Federal-Provincial Meeting of Finance and Health Ministers Ottawa, May 8, 1973
Introduction:
Mr. Lalonde has just explained the modification in the basic federal formula for determining the amount of the federal financial contribution for provincial health care services and substantial improvements in the so-called "risk-sharing" provisions. He has also given assurances that provinces will retain federal sharing now paid under the Canada Assistance Plan when they switch a health or health-related program from a needs test basis to a universal basis.
The federal proposal thus provides for a reasonable rate of growth in basic federal payments. And it includes a risk-sharing provision which takes account of a number of suggestions we have received from provincial governments. Perhaps most importantly, provinces will be free to spend federal payments throughout the entire range of health services, so that they will be able to plan their programs according to their own priorities. This additional flexibility, together with thrust funds, will assist provincial governments in the development of more effective and economical systems of health delivery. The fact that federal payments will no longer be related to costs will also, of course, mean an end to the detailed federal audit.
As I indicated to provincial ministers of finance in a letter of April 18, if provincial governments are now prepared to agree to the formula which Mr. Lalonde has proposed on behalf of the federal government, I would be ready to consider with you in some detail the form of the federal contribution. In this regard, a number of provincial governments have expressed the view that the federal payment for health services should be via a reduction in federal government taxes. This would enable provinces to increase their rates, with no increase in the tax burden borne by Canadians.
Principles Underpinning Tax Transfer
Accordingly, I should like to make a specific proposal to you today. It is predicated on the condition that provinces are able to agree with the new formula approach for determining the annual federal contribution to provincial health care programs. Before outlining the specific details, however, I want to set out the principles which underlie the tax transfer proposal.
First, the size of the reduction in federal taxes must take into account the expected rate of growth in revenues from the tax room being transferred; it must also take account of increase in the federal contribution for health services. Perhaps this is a point which is not well understood and I should make clear what is involved. Suppose the federal government were to cut its taxes today by the exact number of personal income tax points required to cover the federal contribution for health services in this year and provinces were to raise theirs by a commensurate amount. That number of tax points would, in less than a
year, over-compensate provincial governments by a very large amount. The reason, of course, is that the value of tax points is growing more rapidly than the expected rate of growth in provincial spending on health services and the anticipated federal payments for these services.
As a concrete example to illustrate this point, let me take the recent proposal put forward by the Government of Quebec for a 28-point income tax point transfer to cover the federal payment for hospital insurance, medical care and post-secondary education. Our calculations show that such a transfer would, by the end of the decade, yield provincial governments a cumulative sum of more than $10 billion over and above the amount of federal payments otherwise available. Moreover, at that time, the excess payments would be growing at a rate of about $3 billion annually. It was never intended that a transfer of tax room to cover federal obligations under existing shared-cost programs should be used as a mechanism for a large-scale transfer of fiscal revenues from the federal to the provincial level. That is an issue which we have always maintained should be resolved on its own merits, and not determined as a more or less accidental result of new financing arrangements covering shared-cost programs.
Second, we remain convinced that it is in the overriding national interest for the federal government to continue to occupy a large position in the personal income tax field. This is fundamental, if the federal government is to continue to bear the main burden of responsibility for economic stabilization, to maintain harmony in the over-all national tax system, and to fulfill its responsibilities for the distribution of income among Canadians and among the regions of Canada.
Third, as Mr. Lalonde has already mentioned, if the federal government is to cut taxes to pay for its share of health services, this would have to be based upon firm undertakings that the basic principles of the existing hospital and medical legislation remain unaltered. I refer here to the principles relating to the universality and comprehensiveness of services; the accessibility of these services to the Canadian people; their public, non-profit nature; and the portability of coverage for individual Canadians moving from one province to another. The importance of maintaining these conditions has been emphasized in the past and, from earlier discussions, I believe there is a consensus in support of this position.
Let me add one further important point. The transfer of tax room can only be made operative if all provinces accept the new financing arrangements. We cannot see our way clear to implement the necessary tax cut unless it can be applied across the country. Otherwise, there would be different basic levels of federal taxation from province to province. This is a situation which we would regard as injurious to national unity and the growth and efficiency of the national economy.
Details of Proposal
Bearing these principles in mind, we would like to suggest a transfer of tax room in two parts, together wiith a continuation of cash adjustment payments for as long as they may be required.
May 9, 1973

First, we would be prepared to reduce the rate of federal personal income tax by 6 percentage points. These tax points would be equalized to the national average under the existing provisions of the Fiscal Arrangements Act. The federal government would give a firm undertaking to effect this transfer. But, for reasons I shall explain in a moment, we do not think it would be practical, or desirable to make it operative until January 1, 1977. An appropriate cash payment would therefore be continued during this transitional period.
Second, we would be prepared to eliminate the existing federal excise taxes and duties on domestic and imported tobacco products, spirits, brandy, wine and beer. Provincial governments would then be able to move into this tax room without any increase in costs to consumers. It would be possible to implement the federal tax cut effective on January 1, 1975. The additional revenues that provinces could obtain from these revenue sources would also be equalized to the national average. Provincial governments, of course, already obtain large amounts of revenues from these two tax sources. Federal withdrawal would thus enable provinces to consolidate their revenue position in these areas.
Third, to the extent that the value of the tax cut is not sufficient to pay for the federal contribution for health services, as determined under the GNP-escalated formula, the federal government would make this up by a cash adjustment. In due course, and at varying dates, the growth in the yield of the taxes transferred would provide revenues to each province equal to and higher than the federal payment otherwise due.
Mechanics of the Tax Proposal
Let me elaborate a little on the important question of the mechanics of the tax transfers proposed.
With respect to the personal income tax, I must make clear, at the outset, that for reasons which are well known to all of you the federal government will not effect its tax cut through the abatement system. Rather, the tax cut would be implemented through the introduction of new federal and provincial rate schedules. When the federal government reduces its rate, provincial administrations will be able to obtain the federal revenues foregone by increasing their tax rates. There would be no additional burden on taxpayers.
However, as I have already indicated, we do not think it desirable to try to implement this major change in the federal rate structure until January 1, 1977. There are two reasons for this. The first is that Canadian taxpayers have only recently been subject to some fairly extensive changes in the structure of the personal income tax system. This is the first year in which they will have an opportunity to become accustomed to new forms and new schedules. In addition, a number of provincial governments have recently introduced changes in their own personal income tax systems in the form of property tax credits, school tax credits and so forth. We think it is very desirable to give the tax system a chance to settle down before any further major changes are made. Second, by 1977, we will have had some years of experience with the new tax system. We need that experience to obtain more
adequate information respecting the system. That date appears to me as the most appropriate time at which the transfer could be formally effected. Naturally, provinces would be paid in the form of cash until the federal income taxes are cut.
As for the proposal respecting excise levies, the federal government would amend the Excise Act, the Excise Tax Act and the Customs Tariff in order to remove the special excise taxes and duties on tobacco products and alcoholic beverages. This includes the excise element of the customs duties on imports of such goods.
In the case of tobacco products, the repeal of federal excise levies would allow the provinces to increase provincial sales taxes on these goods by an equivalent amount without increasing tobacco prices. The provinces would thus acquire additional revenue equal to the amount of federal revenue foregone.
In the case of spirits and wines, the provinces, by holding constant their retail prices on these beverages, would acquire the federal revenues foregone because of the elimination of the federal excise taxes and duties on these products. The transfer of revenues from spirits and wines would thus be effected through an implicit increase in provincial mark-ups. In provinces where certain Canadian wines are retailed through manufacturers' outlets, the recovery by the province of federal levies on such wines might require the introduction of a special provincial tax.
The transfer of federal revenues on beer could be effected by provinces increasing their levies on breweries simultaneously with the repeal of the federal excise taxes and duties.
I understand that the value of the tax room provided to each province through a repeal of excise taxes and duties would be relatively simple to measure. Excise rates on alcoholic beverages and most tobacco products are expressed as fixed amounts per unit or gallon. Accordingly, the value of the tax room in each province would be determined by multiplying those rates by the quantities sold in each province. I should add that the elimination of excise levies on alcoholic beverages would not mean that federal supervision over quality control in the production of these products would end. The federal government would continue to maintain supervisory personnel in distilleries and breweries to ensure quality control.
We would also propose that any additonal revenues which flow to the provinces as a result of higher provincial tax rates on personal income, alcohol and tobacco, would be equalized automatically under the general equalization formula in the Fiscal Arrangements Act. The amount of equalization would of course be treated as an integral part of the federal payment for health services to the seven provinces receiving equalization.
In the case of Quebec, there is already in place a special 16-point personal income tax abatement which constitutes a part of the federal contribution for hospital insurance in that province. If the provinces agree with our proposal and the federal government goes ahead with a reduction of 6 points of personal income tax, I shall want to consult with the minister of finance for Quebec concerning the future status of the special abatement.

May 9, 1973
Financial Aspects of the Proposed Tax Transfer
I want to say a word now about the financial implications of the proposed transfer of tax room. The year 1975 is the first year in which the federal duties and taxes would be eliminated. In that year, I estimate the value of the proposed transfer of excise tax room would be worth about $1.4 billion, including associated equalization. I estimate this $1.4 billion will be a little more than half the proposed federal contribution for health services in that year. Fiscal year 1977-78 would be the first complete year in the new health financing agreement in which both the excise taxes and personal income tax transfers would be effective. In 1977-78 I estimate that, for the country as a whole, about 85 to 90 per cent of the federal payment will be covered by the tax transfer. This percentage will vary somewhat from province to province, but it would appear that, in 1977-78, all provinces will receive at least 75 per cent of the federal payment through the proposed transfer of tax room.
You are all aware that the value of personal income tax points grows rapidly, whereas revenues from alcohol and tobacco taxes grow relatively less quickly. By combining the two, I believe we have a package which will provide an appropriate rate of growth of revenue to pay for health programs. Over a period of years, as the value of the personal income tax component grows relative to the excise room, the value of the tax cuts by the federal government will gradually reduce the required cash adjustment. In due course, provincial governments can reasonably anticipate that the tax transfer will more than cover the federal commitment.
Of course, I do not want to suggest that provincial governments would have to increase their tax rates by the precise amount of the federal cut. Provinces can raise their levies more or less than the federal reduction, as they see fit, and they obviously could alter the mix between personal income tax or their taxes on alcohol and tobacco.
Our estimates are no more than estimates. It is still not possible to be precise about the yield of the personal income tax under the new tax system. Furthermore, any projections about the future value of tax points are based heavily on estimates respecting the future growth of the economy. If the value of the tax room transferred should grow very rapidly, then the date when the value of tax room exceeds the amount of the federal contribution would arrive sooner. If the growth rate in the tax room being transferred turns out to be less than we estimate, provincial governments will receive larger cash adjustment payments.
Conclusions
Let me summarize the essential points in the federal proposal respecting the formula and the tax transfer. The proposal would enable provincial governments to spend the funds they receive as they see fit. The additional flexibility provided will enable them to introduce and operate more economic and effective ways of delivering health services. The amount of the reduction in federal taxes will, in due course, enable them to administer their programs without direct federal financial support. In fact,
provinces may experience a "surplus" relative to the federal government's financial commitment respecting provincial health costs.
I understand that this subject will be on the agenda of the first ministers' meeting later this month. I recognize that not all of you will be able to comment in detail today on the proposal which I have put before you. However, it would be helpful to get preliminary reactions from you.
I believe that if we can reach an agreement on the federal payment, thus making it possible to implement the tax transfer, we shall have taken a large and important step forward. The winner, as a result, will be the Canadian people-both as taxpayers and recipients of health services.

subtopic: FINANCING FEDERAL AID TO POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION

speechtext:
[The attached statement by Finance Minister John N. Turner to the joint federal-provincial meeting of finance and education ministers responds to a letter from the Honourable Saul Miller, Manitoba Minister of Colleges and University Affairs. Mr. Miller's letter, written on the behalf of the provinces' Council of Education Ministers, proposed a transfer of additional tax points to the provinces to finance post-secondary education.]
I would like to address myself to three points made in the letter: (1) the suggestion that the federal government should transfer additional personal income tax points to the provinces in the form of a tax abatement to finance post-secondary education; (2) that these tax points should be equalized to the value of the tax in the province with the highest yield; (3) the implication that this program should be used as a means to transfer a greater share of revenues from the Government of Canada to provincial governments for general purposes.
The letter outlines the reasons why the transfer of additional tax points is being requested. Essentially, it is argued that a transfer in the form of tax points would avoid interfering with the ability of individual provinces to determine their own priorities. It would also allow provinces greater flexibility to achieve greater efficiency and improvement in services. Finally, it would eliminate the administrative complexities of the present arrangements, related to such things as the definition of shareable costs, settlement of final payments and apparent inconsistencies in practice from province to province.
I might say at the outset that the formula Mr. Faulkner has presented to you this afternoon will overcome the problems just described. Under the new formula, which relates the federal contribution to factors other than actual program operating costs, provinces would be freed from the administrative intrusion that inevitably results when contributions are related to actual program practices and costs. Provinces would have all of the freedom and flexibility they needed to develop their own programs as they see fit.
The suggestion that additional personal income tax points be transferred from the Government of Canada to provincial governments does not appear to me to be justified. At the present time, the 4.357 points of personal income tax and the one point of corporate taxable income.
May 9, 1973

both equalized to the national average, which form part of the federal payment to the provinces, cover about 55 per cent of the federal contribution. The remainder is, of course, paid out in the form of cash to the provinces. We all foresee that the value of these tax points will increase at a more rapid rate than the rates at which post-secondary education costs will rise. As a result, the value of the tax points already abated to provinces will exceed the federal financial commitment in the foreseeable future. From the day this happens, provinces will in effect be receiving an "overpayment", if I may put it that way, for this program. Moreover, the amount of this "overpayment" will increase each year as the value of the tax points increases relative to the increase in program costs.
A major objective on our part, which I believe provincial governments would share, is to establish conditions that allow provinces the freedom and flexibility they are asking for to manage their own programs of post-secondary education, while maintaining a reasonable growth of federal contributions. By a reasonable growth rate, we mean a rate that is roughly commensurate with the growth in the national economy.
The formula proposed, consisting of the 1973-74 actual federal contribution escalated by the rate of growth of the population group 18-24 years of age, together with the 7 per cent escalation factor, will add up to an annual growth of between 9 and 10 per cent in federal contributions. This formula represents a generous contribution towards provincial post-secondary education costs and is somewhat higher than the growth in costs anticipated for the current fiscal year. It provides an adequate margin for improving provincial post-secondary education programs, over and above what might be needed to meet rising prices. A transfer of additional tax points, as I pointed out, would involve a much higher rate of federal contribution and would jeopardize the goal of reasonable growth. Alternatively, the transfer of additional tax points would merely mean that this program was used as a device for transferring resources to the provinces, for purposes other than post-secondary education. I do not see how we could justify such a step on either grounds.
The second point in Mr. Miller's letter I would like to comment on is the suggestion for a new system of equalization based on the province where the yield is highest. The basic principle underlying the general equalization program contained in the Fiscal Arrangements Act, and generally accepted by both recipient and non-recipient provinces alike, is that the lower-income provinces should receive a federal grant to enable them to finance a national average level of services. This is still a valid national policy objective. The suggestion in Mr. Miller's letter is in conflict with this principle. Moreover, I would note that equalization of some tax points to the value in the province with the highest yield, rather than to the national average, value would imply that post-secondary education programs have a higher priority than we may, in fact, be prepared to accord them. I would put these programs in a privileged position vis-a-vis other programs competing for national resources. I fail to see the justification for such special treatment.
The last point I want to comment on is the implication that post-secondary education programs should be used as a means to transfer more tax revenue from the federal to provincial governments in order to meet growing cost pressures. I take it that these "growing cost pressures" relate to programs other than post-secondary education. Recent experience has shown considerable easing in the rate of growth of expenditures on post-secondary education.
If the problem is pressure on government programs generally, it seems to me that the post-secondary education program should not be used as a vehicle for meeting it. Rather the case for more revenues should be argued on its own merits. As I said this morning, it was never intended that a transfer of tax room to cover federal obligations under existing shared-cost programs should be used as a mechanism for a large scale transfer of fiscal resources from the federal to the provincial governments. This morning I proposed transfering all of the excise taxes and duties on tobacco and alcohol plus 6 personal income tax points to the provinces to help in the financing of health programs. I fully appreciate the views and concerns of provinces who have requested tax room to finance well-established programs, and this has been reflected in our proposal this morning. At the same time, we have to move carefully in this direction so as not to erode seriously the ability of the federal government to use the tax system as a major instrument of economic policy.
In this connection, I can only repeat what we have so often maintained in the past: that the federal government has a responsibility to maintain sufficient control over the income tax system to permit it to effectively manage the economy and to achieve a greater degree of equality in the distribution of income between provinces and between individuals.
I might also draw to the attention of our provincial colleagues that the recent federal budget contained three major measures making for larger provincial revenues or tax room. First, the personal income tax was cut substantially, in the order of $1.3 billion, and these amounts have no termination date. Second, the rapid economic upswing that is developing from the budgetary measures will increase provincial revenues in the order of $400 million accumulated over a period of two years. Third, the inclusion in the general equalization system of municipal taxes imposed for local school purposes will add about $190 million beginning this fiscal year to the seven lower-income provinces. In all, I think it fair to say that these moves have assisted provinces during this current year in financing their growing budgets without generalized tax increases.
These conclude my comments on the suggestions in Mr. Miller's letter.

subtopic: THE GUARANTEE OF PROVINCIAL REVENUES

speechtext:
Notes for Remarks by Finance Minister John N. Turner to a Joint Federal-Provincial Meeting of Finance Ministers and Treasurers
You will recall that the revenue guarantee was originally proposed as a device to ensure that provinces, which

May 9, 1973
adopted income tax legislation conforming to that of the federal government, would receive no less in tax revenue under the new system of tax reform than under the previous tax system, had it remained in place. We could not know the precise effects of tax reform, or be certain whether a province would suffer a loss of revenue by adopting the new system.
The best estimates at the time indicated that the tax base upon which new provincial personal income tax rates would be levied would be about 8 per cent lower than the so-called federal "basic tax" employed under the old tax system. Accordingly, our calculations suggested that provinces levying rates in the proportion of 30.5 over 28 of their 1971 rates would be receiving about the same amount of revenue under the new system as under the old. If it turned out that the calculations of the federal government were wrong, and the provinces received more revenue under the new system, they would retain this benefit. On the other hand, if the provincial revenues received from applying the new, higher converted rate to the lower base were less than the amount estimated to be received under the old system, this difference would be made up as part of the guarantee. The guarantee, you recall, covers the combined yields of the personal and corporate income taxes, including associated equalization. Thus, as long as provinces continued to conform to the federal income tax legislation and expressed their provincial income taxes on the federal base, the guarantee would be operative.
I have been reviewing the revenue guarantee in the light of its original intent, and taking account of developments since its inception in January, 1972. I must admit that the guarantee has become an exceedingly complicated issue, both in technical terms but, more importantly, in its broader context. The original intent of the guarantee was to encourage provinces to conform to the new federal income tax legislation. If provinces conformed and expressed their tax rates on the basis of federal tax payable, the federal government was prepared to guarantee the yield of the new system to be at least equivalent to that of the old. To this end, the federal government calculated new converted tax rates, designed to yield revenues equal to the old system and guaranteed that the application of these rates would yield revenues equal to the old system.
It can be argued that the guarantee should not compensate for any changes in the tax system subsequent to January, 1972. If changes did occur to the federal tax base so as to affect provincial revenues, the provincial tax rates ought to be adjusted to yield the same revenues as before the changes, in the manner followed at the beginning of 1972. While these arguments have some merit, I am of the view that the position we have adopted respecting the changes announced for 1972 and 1973 is appropriate.
In the budget of February 19, I proposed a number of changes which would reduce the personal income tax burden on Canadian taxpayers. These included increases in personal expemptions from $1,500 to $1,600 for single persons and from $2,850 to $3,000 for married persons
effective January 1, 1973. I also proposed that the exemptions and tax brackets would be automatically increased each year by reference to changes in the consumer price index. This indexation of the personal income tax system, which is to begin in 1974, is designed to relieve taxpayers of increased income taxes which arise not from gains in productivity, but from the interaction of inflation and the progressive nature of the tax system.
I announced at the time of the budget that the reduction in provincial revenues arising out of the increased exemptions for individual taxpayers would be covered under the provisions of the revenue guarantee contained in part IV of the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act, 1972. This action parallels a similar decision taken in May, 1972 when I announced that the measures reducing both personal and corporation income taxes would also be covered by the guarantee.
Still, the indexation of the personal income tax, to begin in 1974, appears to me to differ in substance from other changes that have been proposed or enacted. In essence, the indexation proposal reduces the tax burden on individuals which arise out of inflationary, not real, gains and adds a greater degree of fairness to the tax system. As a corollary, governments will no longer be able to spend tax money arising from inflationary gains, but will be required to increase tax rates explicitly, in order to carry out more ambitious spending programs.
The indexation proposal was well received by Parliament and by Canadian taxpayers generally. I am not surprised by this reaction, since the proposal constitutes a major advance in the fairness and equity of the tax system. We all recognize that this advance is not without cost. The proposal means that governments will receive somewhat less revenue than they would otherwise have obtained from a continuation of the present system. This is necessary to give meaning to the indexing feature. I would emphasize, however, that the only revenues thereby foregone by governments are those which the tax structure would have imposed on inflationary, and not real, gains in income. Uqcler these circumstances, it seems to me entirely inappropriate for provinces to expect compensation for those foregone revenues. I would not expect provincial governments to ask the federal government to increase its taxes on Canadian taxpayers, who have had their burden relieved by indexation, in order to make payments to provinces, equal to inflationary revenue gains they would have received in the absence of indexing.
Admittedly, the entire subject of the revenue guarantee is complicated, and I will want to consult with each of you over the coming several months, to arrive at some commonly acceptable solution. There is a particularly difficult problem of adjustment for all provinces when the guarantee comes to an end in 1976. I have been giving some further thought to the situation both immediate and forthcoming. In due course, I would want to consult with you with some concrete proposals. Perhaps we will find it advantageous at an appropriate early date to have some technical aspects of the matter explored by our officials.
I would welcome comments from you on this matter.
Thursday, May 10, 1973
